#6864. All the Gifts GQ Editors Want This Holiday Season 2026

As the desk at GQ that handles all things shopping, the GQ Recommends team has developed a rather motley assortment of wants, needs, and highly specific desires. We have good taste, if I may say as much, and no shortage of opinions about what makes a thing worth owning. So this holiday season, I asked everyone to set aside the usual assignments and show me what's on their own wishlists. What follows is an eclectic grab bag of A1 gifts, straight from the folks who spend all year finding the good stuff.

Still got names to cross off? Peruse our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more good stuff worth giving (or keeping).

Years after getting married, I can say with confidence that the best thing about marriage is my wife. But a close second is the set of Sabre Bistrot flatware we received off our registry. A pleasure to hold and behold. And now they make chopsticks, which is unfortunate news for someone afflicted with my particular strain of completism. I have no choice but to finish the set. —MN

I couldn’t in good conscience ask for everything I want from Camiel Fortgens, which is, uh, everything. But this heavy-knit beanie, with the melange yarn and signature raw edges, feels like a reasonable place to start. —MN

It's true, the best radio station on the internet deserves its own hardware. Made in collaboration with tech company Atonemo, this dedicated player has big, tactile buttons for tuning into NTS 1 and 2, a dial for wandering through the Infinite Mixtapes, and the ability to plug straight into my amp. I feel so alive, and I've never been more excited to turn a dial. —MN

Nosying around other people’s bookshelves is a favorite pastime, and I can think of only a few libraries I’d rather rifle through than Luis Barragan’s. I’ve made the pilgrimage to his home and studio in Mexico City, and this new book offers a new look at the peerless architect’s life and influences through the personal collection he kept on his shelves. —MN

You may already know that we love Lady White’s top-tier white T-shirts, but we’re also massive fans of their sweats, especially this superweight hoodie. And when they say superweight, they mean it. I’ve own the zip-up version, and it's basically a winter coat. This will become my dog-walking hoodie, my 6 A.M. stroll to the bodega hoodie, and the late-night walk back from the cinema hoodie. —JB

Back in high school, some homies and I thought of ourselves as future producers. The music was terrible and thankfully is lost in the ether somewhere on SoundCloud, but despite those early attempts, I still find sampling a fascinating part of music. It’s a way to shut off the brain and think about songs in a new way. I doubt the music will be any better than it was back in the day, but I’ll have fun acting like Jamie XX or Nicolas Jaar, at least. —JB

I’m a pen-and-paper guy. You will often catch me feverishly jotting down thoughts in the middle of a meeting. I’ve recently needed to retire my old Moleskine notebook and found myself doing a deep dive into reusable leather-bound book holders that you can treat like a modular journal. You can add in different types of notebooks, calendars, and daily planners—the possibilities are endless. —JB

There comes a time in every man's life when he fancies himself a barista and thinks he should dedicate some time to learning how to pull a damn good espresso. I am that man, and the delusions are more errant than you would expect. Because I drink so much coffee, I’ve convinced myself I might as well get good at making it. —JB

As much as I don’t want to admit that I overindex on outerwear, my closet tells the truth. It’s so full that I can’t even shift any of the hangers without taking one of them out first. But that won’t stop me from eyeing this gorgeous coat from Auralee. It’s everything I want in a coat: dramatically long, artfully faded, and a deep black colorway. Now I’ll just have to find a new coat rack. —GO

I saw this bad boy in a shop and was so drawn to it. The colors are just right, the size is great, and the material is ultra-sturdy, but on this day, the devil on my shoulder told me not to get it that day. I came to my senses and came back the next day only to find that the tote was sold out. Hence why I’ve got it on my wish list because I believe in second chances and miracles. —GO

This little thing is a clever ear warmer that can be worn as is or can be slipped over the bill of your favorite hat. It’s silly and weird and cool and totally unnecessary. And yet, I would not be mad if this made its way into my stocking. —GO

I’ve always wanted a true Neapolitan-style jacket and getting to try on some of Natalino’s pieces in person during a pop-up in NYC has only stoked the fire. From the hand-stitched entails to the soft shoulders to the absolutely supreme fit, there’s no better jacket in my mind. —GO

No, I am not a ne'er-do-well Italian playboy loath to step into a leadership position at my dad's sprawling imports company. Yes, I would like to dress like one. —AG

Leave it to the vintage fiends in Japan to turn up a version of JCPenney’s canonical Big Mac flannel—the greatest flannel ever made, FYI—that might actually be worth the asking price. —AG

Okay, okay, okay. Once the sticker shock has worn off, think about how good of a boy I’ve been this year… —AG

You could drop $100K on leg-lengthening surgery and then rebuild your jeans rotation from scratch. Or you could just buy La Botte Gardiane’s naturally height-enhancing boots, which look great with the jeans you already own. —AG

I used to question whether the Eadem hype was another fad born of bloated influencer budgets, but dude. This balm is legit. I want every single color. You should get this for your girl for the holidays. If you’re scared of picking colors for her, opt for “Butter Mochi” (clear! unscented!) or “Sakura Shaved Ice,” a light pink that complements nearly every lip combo under the sun. —MH

I was treating my guy to his first ever foray into Buck Mason when I clocked a store employee wearing the Roper Jean and immediately lost the plot RE: which T-shirt the boy was trying on next. The silhouette! The wash! The contrast stitching! The complimentary Buck Mason tailoring for my stubby little legs! A girl can dream. A girl is still dreaming. Someone please gift this to me. —MH

Confessions of an adult seasonal allergies sufferer: I open the windows to air out my apartment despite knowing that that’s just welcoming the allergens into my home. Practical people might say I should address the issue at the root, but where’s the whimsy in that? Wouldn’t capitalism prefer that I purchase a solution to my problem instead? —MH

It took only one year at GQ and one “welcome to the team” bottle of D.S.&Durga to turn me into a fragrance fiend. For my bank account’s sake, I made a No New Fragrances vow earlier this summer … but gifts don’t count as breaking that pledge. Also, I really need a winter scent; my beloved Eau Splendide is more of a summer gal. —MH

I already own a bottle of Naked Dance, and it’s dangerously close to empty, which is the highest compliment I can give a fragrance. Well, the second highest. The first is how often I’m asked what fragrance I’m wearing, and I’m not ready to give that up. It’s a cult pick from a tiny niche house, right down to the cap, which is handmade from wood scraps and resin, exactly the kind of detail I can’t resist. —AH

I’m a vintage obsessive at heart, and this bracelet has that worn-in, one-of-a-kind look I’m always drawn to. Pyrite is also known as fool’s gold, and frankly, I’d be a fool not to want it. —AH

A good belt is the most underrated piece in any outfit, and my studded belt collection could always use one more. I’ve reached the point where I pick my outfits around my belts, not the other way around, and this one already has a few looks planned. The most practical gift on my list? I think so. —AH

All fall I’ve been hunting for the perfect pair of cords, mostly because I’m notorious for wearing the same pants almost every day. These feel like they walked straight out of a ’70s record sleeve, with that soft, slouchy fit. They’d slot into my current wardrobe perfectly, and finally give my usual pair a break. —AH

I love a gift you can give and secretly steal for yourself. This bathrobe is a “thoughtfu” gift for your partner that you’ll get to commandeer when they’re not looking. Two for the price of one really. You’re welcome! —LP

It’s a cliché, but the best gifts are the ones you wouldn’t buy for yourself but desperately want. And who doesn’t want a chic, soft, luxurious, well-designed towel? No one, is the answer. Tekla has a knack for unexpected color combinations that should feel wrong but somehow feel so right (this pink and brown combo is excellent)—a mood booster for any bathroom. Oh, and they’re unisex, making them a handy option when you have a last-minute gift to give. —LP

There is a myth that shower gel, or “smellies” as we call them in the UK (I’m British), are thoughtless gifts. I disagree. A luxury shower gel will add a little something extra to your morning routine, or someone else’s, and is a crowd pleaser for secret santa. This specific wash I can attest also smells incredible. —LP

Last holiday season, I treated my mother to a pair of Jenni Kayne cashmere socks. Since then, she’s never looked back and now has an expectation that Christmas = cashmere. She deserves it, so I’m happy to oblige (I may as well buy myself a pair at the checkout whilst I’m at it). They make a great gift for anyone who loves a cozy weekend at home or wants something luxurious to slip into after a day of hiking or skiing (my personal favourite time to treat my feet). —LP

A couple of decades ago, Helmut Lang was the place to go for a more city-minded denim jacket. And while those pieces still do numbers on the second-hand market, I’ve always found them a touch too fitted. So imagine my relief to discover this roomier Kaptain Sunshine take, which still feels special (and office-appropriate) due to its pleats, dark color, and smart single pocket. —LC

As a teenager, I was completely taken by this scent. Then, throughout my twenties, I tried all of the nicher body washes I thought I was meant to like. The ones that smelled like herb gardens, cedar forests, or sometimes… nothing at all. But following a recent, delayed flight-induced spin around Duty Free, I was reunited with Re-Charge Black Pepper. Please, kind gifters, reunite me with even more of it. —LC

Not just a stunning book about jazz and America in the 1960s, but also hundreds of pages of incredible style. I’m hoping to deepen my understanding of the music over the holidays, and know it would only help to be leafing through this as I do so. —LC

As with the Molton Brown above, I’m done surveying the market: I feel my best in these! And I’d wager the men (and women) in your life likely do too. —LC

Genetics haven’t exactly done some of us any favors in the under-eye department (me, I'm talking about me), but this eye cream levels the playing field. It works beautifully for me, and it’s exactly the kind of splurge that makes a great gift. —EH

Experiment is one of the most exciting skincare brands I’ve come across lately, with a thoughtfully edited lineup that doesn’t try to do too much. Its new mini set is a great introduction, featuring what I think is an underrated ingredient: glycerin. It helps skin hold onto moisture, which is exactly what my thirsty skin craves in these drier times. —EH

Vitaly has been on my radar for years, and I’ve had my eye on more than few of its chains and rings. It just launched an Art Deco line, which is a glorious mix of classic style and signature industrial Vitaly edge. While a lot of the larger statement pieces are on my wishlist, the Tier Chain feels like a daily driver and a statement piece at the same time. —EH

Once we get through the joyfully chaotic holidays, the new year calls for rest and relaxation. While cozy socks and a soft throw are always welcome gifts, this blanket feels like an ultimate upgrade. Weighted for gentle relaxing pressure and heated for warmth even in the chilliest rooms. Sounds like a recipe for the sweetest of dreams! —EH

#6857. RIP to LIV, the Golf League No One Ever Really Cared About

The most remarkable thing about the era of LIV Golf, a five-year run characterized by near-parodic blunders and missteps, is that leadership and its public-facing talent don’t appear to have learned any lessons from their many failures.

From the beginning, the upstart league, established in 2021 as a rival to the dominant PGA Tour, was plagued by its own ineptitude. It’s only fitting—after LIV’s newfound lifeline, private investment firm BC Partners, reneged on a $300 million investment—that the brand’s figureheads are now celebrating the end by taking a victory lap. Tone-deaf doesn’t begin to describe it.

LIV CEO Scott O’Neil—who took over for original boss and Major winner Greg Norman in January of 2025 and was faced with finding new cash flow after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund announced in April that it would no longer finance the operation—clearly exists in a different reality than our own. “Together, our team delivered world-class individual and team competitions across five continents, built a global business, secured pathways to The Open and U.S. Open… and built a league capable of attracting both elite and rising talent from around the world,” he said in a statement late last week. It’s unclear if the farewell tour will continue, though, an even newer report suggests that BC is looking to purchase a bankruptcy loan from LIV’s current owners. If this Hail Mary works, LIV’s future would look much different than the one O’Neil has promised.

Another way to look at it? One of LIV’s biggest accomplishments was that the league, despite its intentions to diversify the game and bring fun back into a sport that had come to personify privilege and exclusivity, inadvertently consolidated the PGA Tour’s power as a monopolistic behemoth now primed to solidify its status as the only league in town. They helped usher in a new era of leadership and investment for the Tour, including the introduction of CEO Brian Rolapp, who is by all accounts the most well-liked and accomplished boss it’s had in quite some time.

LIV also managed to tarnish the reputations of its biggest stars. Jon Rahm, who was vehemently opposed to the dog and pony show when it was announced, only to sheepishly take a bag of blood money so big his great grandchildren will never have to work a day in their lives, is now one of the game’s great “What If?” stories. Prior to the US Open at Brookline Country Club in June 2022, the defending champion was asked about his thoughts on the upstart league. “Money is great,” he said. But Rahm and his wife thought about it further. “Will our lifestyle change if I got $400 million? No, it will not change one bit.” Just over a year later, he defected to LIV.

Then there’s Phil Mickelson, who was poised to become a fixture of the American Ryder Cup team and widely considered a shoo-in to hold a cushy job as an analyst for golf’s biggest broadcasting events. Upon joining the league, he admitted in a conversation with Alan Shipnuck that Saudi Arabia was a terrible bedfellow. (Shipnuck and Mickelson have disagreed over whether the comments were on or off the record.) “They killed Khashoggi and have a horrible record on human rights. They execute people over there for being gay,” he explained. But there was a caveat: LIV was simply a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to reshape how the PGA Tour operates.” Miraculously, he got that part right.

Prize money on the PGA Tour is greater than ever, the Tour’s main events have recalibrated, and its season-ending championship series has been completely reimagined. Mickelson won’t be allowed within 100 miles of it.

The league’s biggest attraction, Bryson DeChambeau, is theoretically the worst-situated of the game’s many turncoats, though he’s probably more excited about growing his YouTube channel than he is about playing golf anyway. No one’s put their reputation on the line for this gaggle of buffoons quite like DeChambeau, who spoke proudly about how LIV was “growing the game” and “bringing team golf to the world.” This past weekend, he shared a statement on the dissolution of LIV. “I still believe in team golf,” he wrote. “It may look different in the future, but I still believe it’s essential to growing the game.” A loyal foot soldier, even from the grave.

It was always about the money. Nothing more, nothing less. This was a cash grab of epic proportions, and golfers not good enough to earn their keep on the PGA Tour took a life raft and briefly found themselves in possession of luxury superyachts. Then, low tide left them holding bags of cash and not much else. Was it worth it? For most of these golfers, probably. They were past their primes when LIV began; they’re still past the primes now, and just a helluva lot richer.

The league positioned itself as a disruptor, and disrupted so poorly that they’ve turned the PGA Tour into the strongest version of itself we’ve seen since Tiger Woods was at his peak. All that bloviating about the good of LIV Golf from its loudest talking heads is a bunch of nonsense.

It’s hard to tell if these statements are one last line of defense or more genuine delusion from LIV’s last advocates. They came in with the idea of sticking it to the PGA Tour, which at the time was facing bleak circumstances, bogged down in nonsense before redirecting its energy towards batting this gnat into extinction. Ultimately, LIV helped the PGA Tour save itself.

Now it’s gone for good, and five billion dollars later, we’re not gonna remember a damn thing about it. Not the players, not the leadership, and surely not all the ways they supposedly grew the game while merely growing their own bank accounts.

#6853. How Martine Rose Became Menswear’s Secret Weapon

After much speculation, the fashion rumors were true: Martine Rose is officially Balenciaga’s next creative director. It’s undoubtedly her biggest job yet—and a historic appointment: she is the first woman creative director to lead the French house. Rose succeeds Valentino vet Pierpaolo Piccioli, whose departure after just three seasons was announced yesterday. This is a major moment for the British-Jamaican designer, who has spent nearly two decades building a namesake label that wields outsize influence.

Rose has long occupied a curious position in menswear: a designer’s designer with a devoted following of both high-fashion heads and the streetwear obsessed. Since launching her eponymous brand in 2007, she’s developed an unmistakable visual language of playful styling, graphic-driven sportswear, offbeat tailoring, and covetable sneaker collabs. Her clothes take the familiar and make it strange, infusing everyday garments with humor, a touch of romance, and occasionally an ugly-chic sensibility: think square-toed loafers, chap-covered suit trousers, and soccer jerseys with lace-up fastenings. The results can be loud, wildly stylish, and routinely fun.

“I’ve always been drawn to the way men are told to dress,” the designer told GQ in 2023. She’s been on a mission to subvert those conventions ever since.

On the Martine Rose runway, sportswear and tailoring regularly share the spotlight. Much of that sensibility comes from her ability to borrow from and fuse London’s historic subcultures: ravers and club kids, football fanatics and nattily dressed mods. She tends to embrace the unusual and eccentric rather than focusing on making everything read as conventionally stylish. One look from a recent collection featured a swishy track jacket tucked into straight-leg blue jeans, and another paired a perfectly tailored coat with athletic shorts and knee-high socks. In Rose’s universe, there is no wrong way to mix and match. That’s part of her charm.

That sensibility eventually caught the eye of Demna during his decade-long tenure as Balenciaga’s creative director. The firebrand Georgian designer reached out to Rose in 2015, and she spent the next three years as a menswear consultant for the house during a high-profile era defined by supersized proportions and outlandish accessories. The blazers were big and the boots were bigger, but the star power of the celebrities who wore them was the biggest of all.

Rose is no stranger to dressing famous people. Her clothes have landed on some of the most photographed men in the world: Drake, Timothée Chalamet, Bad Bunny, A$AP Rocky. Perhaps her most visible endorsement came at the 2025 Super Bowl, when Kendrick Lamar strutted around the halftime show in a custom red, white, and blue leather varsity jacket designed by Rose. (In 2023, the rapper had boasted about how he wears “Martine when I board jets” on the Baby Keem track “The Hillbillies”; a year later, he sported several of her designs in his “Not Like Us” video.) Over the years, Rose has become one of the rare designers whose collections are covered by both Vogue and Hypebeast, a testament to her appeal across fashion’s various tribes. She’s been a fixture at London Fashion Week, and made her Milan debut in 2024. She has two hit Supreme collaborations under her belt. When Nike came calling, Rose produced remixed versions of the Shox (which Lamar wore while he accepted three Grammys in 2023) and Monarch sneakers—turning two of the Swoosh’s most divisive silhouettes into lustworthy objects. Tommy Hilfiger enlisted her for a collection centered on the streetwise style of Tommy Jeans in the ’90s. Brands know she can deliver the goods.

Which brings us back to the Balenciaga appointment. Rose obviously knows the house, or at least Demna’s vision for it—a vision that brought meme-worthy fashion but also massive creative and commercial success. A statement from Luca de Meo, CEO of Kering (the French luxury group that owns Balenciaga), included all the boilerplate press language about innovation, creativity, and culture. More crucially, Rose has proven she can make familiar clothes feel fresh, taking what guys are already wearing and turning them into something surprising and covetable. The question is now what Rose will be able to do with the resources of a global luxury powerhouse at her disposal. She’s spent much of her career building her own idiosyncratic world at Martine Rose. At Balenciaga, she’ll find herself on a much bigger stage with a vast audience and a completely new rulebook.

In 2020, when discussing her reputation as something of an underground darling, Rose told GQ: “I’ve never really wanted to be part of a big thing. Anything that is mainstream—since I was small—hasn’t really appealed to me.” Six years later, she’s earned one of the biggest jobs in fashion. There’s great fun in evolution, too.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

We’re calling it: 2026 was the year of makeup. After many years of clean girl beauty and an emphasis on minimalism, it’s time to explore colors and self-expression again. This year’s best products go far beyond the typical mascara or run-of-the-mill concealer. Our testers raved about a brow pencil that relies on friction to amp up volume, blushes that looked natural and stayed put for hours, and lip stains that mimicked popsicle-like shades. For all of this and more, keep reading below for our 2026 Future of Beauty winners. We found 26 (the most ever!) color cosmetics worth your attention, spanning lips, eyes, face, and even nails.

For anyone looking to extend the life of their manicure without a trip to the salon, these ultra-thin tips strike an impressive balance between durability and a natural-looking length and finish. Our tester said they were easy to shape and blend seamlessly: “I especially love how thin they look and feel. They give you a little extra length and structure without feeling bulky.” Better yet, the set lasted for weeks and was easy to apply and remove at home.

Charlotte Tilbury Airbrush Flawless Long-Wear Blur Concealer

Downsize your makeup touch-up bag with this dual-sided product that allows you to precisely line, fill, and blur your lips in one go. “In the age of lip combos, this makes it super easy without carting around multiple items,” our tester said.

This elegant stylo blurs, plumps, and adds shine to lips, making them look fuller and richer. Westman Atelier Suprême Bio-Complex Liquid Foundation

This just might be the first foundation formula with exosomes and peptides for skin renewal, in addition to amino-coated powders that replace skin-clogging silicones. Our tester went in skeptical and came out a convert. “I’ve eschewed foundation for most of my adult life. Our tester said, “I loved the shiny blush look that this gave to my skin and, bonus, it looks great on my cheeks and lips.”

YSL Skin Affair Soft Glow Cushion Foundation

An innovative way to improve no-makeup-makeup, this compact delivers foundation in a pre-soaked, spring-loaded sponge. Our tester praised the “good-skin-like” effect and appreciated the broad range of skin tones.

Like a liquid bandage or pimple patch for your nails, a swipe of this liquid forms a protective barrier, fusing damaged areas and dry ridges. Our tester used this on her nails after a gel manicure gone awry and “was genuinely surprised by how well it strengthened and protected them. They look as good as new.”

Buff Beauty Restore Nail Strengthening Serum

This brush-on serum, which dries down nearly instantly, is infused with squalane, amino acids, and biotin to help restore damaged nails. “I’m not good about my cuticles and nails, if I’m being totally honest,” our tester admitted. “I usually just hope a hand cream is enough for them. But after a really damaging round of gel, my nail beds basically needed mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, and this strengthener delivered. I keep it next to my desk and put it on during any lulls in my day. My nails are so much stronger and my cuticles look healthy.”

#6849. 50 Marathons in 24 Days. Men Are Inventing Extreme Physical Challenges for the Hell of It

For more than 18 days straight this past May, Mason Wright woke up every morning at 5 a.m. and ran laps around a track at a high school in Layton, Utah. The early-spring air was typically crisp, and the smell of dew-covered grass reminded him of childhood. By the time students would arrive for class, he’d have run 10 miles. At lunch, he kept running. And when student athletes came out for after-school track practice he would still be there, running alongside them. When the sun finally set over the mountains, he’d crawl into a van parked beside the field, sleep as much as he could, and do it all over again. He ran through freezing mornings that left frost on the ground and rainstorms that flooded the track, leaving his feet so waterlogged that his skin split open.

When Wright finished his extended sprint, he became the third person in the world to run 1,000 fairly consecutive miles around a track, a project he embarked upon because, as he puts it, “I wanted something that genuinely sounded impossible.”

Mason Wright camped nearby a high school track to complete a self-assigned challenge of running 1,000 consecutive miles in a row.

When Wright finished his extended sprint, he became the third person in the world to run 1,000 fairly consecutive miles around a track.

“I wanted something that genuinely sounded impossible,” Wright says of the project.

Wright isn’t the only one with an appetite for the absurd. There’s now a never-ending slew of guys inventing and completing preposterous physical challenges, often with elaborate, self-imposed rules meant to make them as miserable as humanly possible. Many have teams chronicling every grueling mile and setback online. If they manage to pull it off the challenge, they emerge as semi-viral niche sports heroes in their corner of the fitness internet. In 2020, ultramarathoner and Navy Seal David Goggins launched his annual 4x4x48 challenge, inviting his followers to run four miles every four hours for 48 hours. In December 2025, UK-based athlete Travis Kerry set the world record for longest nonstop bear crawl after bear crawling 50 kilometers (31 miles) across the streets of London, and nine months later Kevin Ocipeka from Germany burpee broad-jumped his way 26.2 miles along a track in 155 hours, 44 minutes, and 51 seconds—longer and faster than anyone had burpeed before.

“There’s this flywheel effect of extreme one-upmanship going on on social media,” says Michael Ceely, a psychotherapist and high-performance coach who works with athletes.

But beyond bragging rights, why are men motivated to push themselves to such dire limits? And what, exactly, are they getting out of it?

Many of the men I spoke to for this piece are drawn to the unknown. Once they have an idea, they hyperfixate on it until they accomplish it. Professional mountain biker Matt Jones says the concepts come from just about anywhere. “That’s how my brain works,” he says. He can’t drive past a rooftop or construction crane without wondering whether he could ride it or jump off it. “It doesn’t take long before you start going down a rabbit hole of crazy ideas, and then actually becoming obsessed with them enough to wanna do them,” he says. For the stunt he pulled off in November 2025, he spent months calculating the precise timing needed to jump through the open trailers of two trucks traveling in opposite directions, with only a split-second margin for error.

Matt Jones in Sweden strategizing for his 2025 ‘Through’ project, in which he jumped through the open trailers of two trucks traveling in opposite directions.

Matt Jones performed a world first jumping between two moving trucks.

William Goodge, an ultrarunner who embarked on the arduous task of running 50 marathons in 50 states in 24 days this October, is similarly attracted to the uncertainty that comes with each challenge. “If I wasn’t scared by it, I wouldn’t be enthusiastic,” he says. “That’s the whole point in this journey for me.” His quest, which culminated at this year’s NYC marathon, was nearly as logistically challenging as it was physically demanding. A flight delay or bad weather could have set him back a few hours, potentially derailing his entire schedule. On four of the days, he needed to run three marathons with only short stretches of rest or travel between them.

The thrill of chasing a near-impossible goal can seem grim once you’re in the thick of it, though, and that misery is equally part of the appeal. Kerry had dreamed of earning a Guinness World Record since childhood, and when he saw someone bear-crawl a marathon, he decided to take the record even further: 31 miles, compared to 26. He tested the movement on a treadmill, taking 20 minutes to cover a single kilometer. It was, he says, “the hardest fucking thing I’ve ever done.” But he figured if he could do one kilometer, he could do 50. “It’s just one 50 times, and I just need to get better at it,” he says.

Yet halfway through his bear crawl across the cobbled streets of London, rain was coming down, his hands were cold, and he was wearing a pair of garden gloves he had cut the fingertips off to prevent his palms from getting torn on the pavement. “One of my best mate’s jobs the whole time was squeezing water like a literal udder out the end of my gloves,” he says. Kerry thought about calling it quits. “Even though I physically wasn’t at the end of my limit, mentally I was like, I just can’t do this anymore,” he says.

UK-based athlete Travis Kerry completed a 50-kilometer bear crawl across the cobbled streets of London in 2025.

Kerry still hasn't regained feeling in his fingertips after completing the challenge. “I don’t know if that’s ever gonna come back,” he says. “A small price to pay.”

His coach could tell he was losing steam, so she told him to stand up and scream. “I went to the edge of Tower Bridge and screamed the word ‘fuck’ as loud as I possibly could,” he says. The release felt incredible. He got back down on his hands and feet and kept crawling.

Despite the sense of accomplishment they represent, these feats can come at a serious physical cost. Both Wright and Kerry say they may have suffered permanent nerve damage after their massive efforts. Wright, who ran 400 miles on stress fractures, says the pain that would take over his body was “unbearable.” Kerry hasn’t regained feeling in his fingertips. “I don’t know if that’s ever gonna come back,” he says. “A small price to pay.” Jones acknowledges that he’s spent most of his most epic moments in the last 10 years in physical pain. “I think there’s a limit to the force you can take and the number of years you can take it for,” he says.

The men who do these challenges put their bodies through hell in the search for personal growth and self-discovery. Take Goodge. He began running after losing his mom to cancer. “I wanted to feel physical pain to deal with the mental and spiritual pain of what I was going through,” he says. Compared with what she endured, he says, his own discomfort seems trivial. “I’m doing it in her honor. I’m doing it for Stand Up to Cancer. I can carry on. I’ve got no excuse not to take another step.”

Wright also found himself confronting the grief of losing his father when he was younger during his 1,000-mile run. “When you lose someone close to you, your world stops, but the world around you continues,” he says. “You almost feel like you’re stuck in time.” Running endless laps around the same track while the students’ lives continued brought that feeling back. “It forces you to let go of these things or else you’ll go more crazy,” he says.

Matt Valaoras, who holds hours-long planks at music festivals and sporting events, started planking as a way to manage his anxiety. As a college student, he could only plank for 45 seconds, but he added on time every day until he could hold it for several hours. As he’s held his core steady through rough conditions (the worst of which was a swarm of bugs biting him while he planked the duration of a Savannah Bananas baseball game), he’s “stacked the evidence” that he can handle anything that’s thrown at him—physical or otherwise. “I can confidently say, ‘Okay, I can do this because I, I did that, and it was worse than I expected,’” he says.

Ceely says it’s common that physical suffering can sometimes be a socially acceptable way for men to process emotional suffering. “Men have a hard time expressing weakness or vulnerability or saying ‘I just feel bad, period,’” he says. “They want to say, ‘Here’s what I did to fix it.’ Which, in a way, is a healthy coping mechanism. It’s better than being depressed.”

Valaoras acknowledges that this is part of the equation for him. “For a lot of guys, myself included, it’s easier to exhaust yourself physically than explain what’s exhausting you mentally. I’ve definitely used exercise as a way to avoid confronting things emotionally.” Nevertheless, he says that following some kind of physical exertion, he feels more comfortable opening up.

Meanwhile, Kerry says that he uses his emotional suffering as a way of fueling his physical feats. “One who chooses suffering is choosing to use their brain’s deflection mechanism to channel that emotional suffering into physical capabilities,” he says. He references the so-called pain cave—a term that many distance runners have used to describe the most miserable moments of an event, when the brain and body start to wear thin. “By focusing on that emotional trigger,” he says, that “becomes the person’s ‘why’.”

This form of emotional release can create a powerful cycle of anticipation and reward—encouraging more and more challenges. “You get adrenaline, endorphins, dopamine,” Ceely says. “There’s a physiological kind of addiction that can start just because you’re human and you’re wired that way.”

And it becomes a lot harder to stop if you have an audience expecting an encore. While most of the athletes I spoke to insisted they would still be doing these challenges if no one was watching, social media introduces pressure and expectations; it “moves the goalposts because the wilder the idea is, the more it sets the standards and moves the bar,” says Jones. Wright acknowledges that you can’t “run these miles and post about it on social media without some ego involved.” As he planned his track run, he was set on doubling the stakes of his last challenge, which was a 421-mile run across Utah. “800 miles isn’t cool, so it had to be 1,000,” he says.

Jones says he wouldn’t attempt his most outlandish stunts without the pressure to hold onto his brand sponsorships or please the fans in his comment sections. He, unlike most men who we spoke to for this piece, is a professional Red Bull athlete, whose livelihood in part depends on pulling off these spectacles. “Would I jump through two moving trucks just for a laugh? Probably not,” he says. “No, I wouldn’t at all.” He nevertheless enjoys his audience’s admiration. “I guess that’s vanity in a way, isn’t it?” he says. “But it’s also the currency of what we do.”

None of these men seem particularly interested in finding a comfortable stopping point. Wright says he has yet to find his limit. Valaoras has world records attempts in mind. Goodge doesn’t plan on slowing down.

“I want to be on the edge. How close can we get without falling off?” Goodge says. “How close to the sun can we fly, like Icarus, and not get burnt?”

#6844. 13 Best Bathrobes for Men 2026: Reviewed by GQ

The best bathrobes for men will turn your modest apartment into a luxury spa in two seconds flat. Sadly, you'll still have to acquire all the relevant permits before you can charge randos for the home massage experience, but that's okay—a swaddly robe is more of a solo thing anyway.

The point: If you're gonna treat yourself to a robe, the robe has to treat you right, too. That means avoiding the cheap-o glorified towels with scratchy materials that just end up pilling after a couple washes. What you actually want is the creme de la creme of men’s bathrobes, the ones kitted out with the fluffiest, softest materials that take it from a mere post-shower dry-off to soul-filling self-care.

To help you in your quest for relaxation supremacy, we tested a slew of bathrobes to find the best of the best, which you'll find the below. While you're here, be sure to check out our guide to the best pajamas.

Imagine stepping out of the shower, wrapping yourself in a plush, thick towel... and then never having to take it off. Brooklinen’s best-selling towels are a mainstay of our home coverage, and the DTC brand's robes employ the same tricks of of the trade: absorbent, piled Turkish cotton repackaged into a calf-length, unisex bathrobe that feels as good as it looks. If ensconcing yourself in cloud-like, towel-caliber cotton isn't doing it for you, extra deep pockets to hide your snacks coupled with those eye-grabbing botanical stripes alone are worth the price of admission.

Quince is in the business of providing luxurious staples at non-luxury price tags. Its robe, one that feels like it could've been hung inside a five-star hotel room's closet, fits the bill. It's constructed from an ultra-soft long-staple cotton, complemented with two patch pockets for throwing in your hands (or the television remote) with a simple-to-use sash for making sure no one's getting a peek at your unsightly goods.

You can cancel that ritzy spa appointment: you don’t actually need to leave the house to score the type of restorative treatment that leaves you feeling refreshed and ready to dive back into your inbox—until, like, Wednesday. Turns out, all you need to cultivate peak spa vibes is a peak spa robe, like Onsen's deceptively absorbent, quick-drying silky Supima cotton number. Wearable in any climate, just looking at this cushy long robe from your steamy shower will set your mind at ease, and the extra-chunky waffle weave—cozy, but not clingy—more than justifies the price, especially when you consider the money you'll save not booking that retreat in the Alps.

If the de facto brand for cool-guy jammies doesn't make you want to cancel your plans and post up at home, its royally fluffy bathrobes will. The Scandi loungewear whisperers at Tekla cut their classic bathrobe from a soft-yet-sturdy midweight pile that’s intentionally slinky, so you can sashay from the bedroom to the kitchen fridge like you’re waltzing down a runway. There are, of course, generously-sized pockets for stashing your phone, remote, sundry snacks, etc. But the real selling point is the range of 19 (!) hyper-tasteful colors it's available in. The only con: limiting yourself to just one.

Dusen Dusen's playful takes on homewares and home decor make it the brand you turn to for something that'll have your houseguests going, “where'd you get that from?” Maybe you won't be wearing a robe in front of said guests, but they can admire its beauty when it's hanging in your bathroom. These printed robes are super plush for post-bath drying sessions, and cozy enough to accidentally fall asleep in while you're sitting on the couch waiting for your hair to dry.

There are robes you dry in, robes you lounge in, and then robes like this: an option meant to live in like you own a McMansion, smoke cigars every night, and enjoy a dram of scotch to “take the edge off.” This Derek Rose cotton robe has a satin-like finish, with a subtle stripe detail that gives it more of a pop than just a regular old blue colorway. The white piping also adds a bit more flair to what could otherwise be a boring robe, and three patch pockets help you tote your things around if you don't have anything going on under there.

Reigning Champ, the Vancouver-based brand behind some of our all-time favorite sweats, has been giving us the warm and fuzzies since we first pulled on its stellar heavyweight hoodie. So imagine our delight when Canada's foremost fleece whizzes brought their particular set of skills to the humble bathroom robe, juicing up the silhouette in the same loopback cotton-jersey that makes their loungewear so great. Wear this terry cloth robe while catching up on the Great British Bake Off from the comfort of your couch—and to make the inevitable trip to the grocery store for miscellaneous pie ingredients immediately afterwards.

This is type of robe you throw on when you want to toast things up but have zero plans to leave the house and therefore refuse to put on "actual" clothes. It has a sweet shawl collar and a full length that gives you all the cozy coverage you want.

What's better than sleeping on a cloud? Being swaddled in one while you slowly meander aorund your apartment. The Parachute robe offers a barely there feel, made possible thanks to its four-ply gauze construction. This one has side-seam pockets that make it easy to slip into

Hommey's catalog of cheerful colors and patterns help the brand stand out, but they're more than just nice to look at. They're made of a plush 100% cotton terry fabric that's as cozy as it gets and cut with a comfortable but un-sloppy silhouette. And while so many other robes use a shawl collar, we love that this one features an indulgently huge notch lapel.

Missoni's unmistakable and kaleidoscopic chevron patterns make for a suite of riche robes that telegraphs your bathroom is full of fancy soaps and lotions. Cut from an all-cotton French terry with a velour-like brushed hand, we'd understand if you'd never want to leave your home.

You may not live in a palazzo in Florence, but Brunello's rakish robe will make you feel like you do. The only thing missing? A cheeky cigar.

A Purple Label look, for Polo prices. Thank you, Ralph.

Material: A lot of fabric is about to touch your naked body, so you better make sure your robe feels good. Higher quality fabrics lead to higher price tags, but we found that it's worth it considering your whole body is about to be swaddled in it. For robes, cotton is the preferred fabric, and there are three common types: Egyptian cotton is the softest and plushes, Turkish cotton is known to be fast-drying, and supima cotton is just as soft as Egyptian cotton with the same quick-dry properties as Turkish. Lastly, you'll also see a lot of waffle weaves, which is mostly a design choice. Not only does it lend a certain look, we also like it because it's extremely absorbent and dries quickly.

Features: Robes don't offer too much in the features department, but at a bare minimum, find a robe with pockets. Two is probably the norm, with some offering a treasured third in the form of a chest pocket. Waist ties keep everything hidden and secure underneath, while some robes offer the option to remove them. And while maybe not a “feature” we chose to highlight robes that come in a variety of prints, patterns, and colors, because bone white robes for everyone isn't exactly fun.

Sizing: Shopping for robes is a lot like shopping for clothes: You need to find something that fits. We preferred to highlight robes that were size inclusive, in that a wide selection of sizes were available. Do note that some of the robes here feature combo sizes, which could make it difficult to figure out which option correlates to the typical shirts you'd wear. Take advantage of any size guides to really help you lock in your correct sizing.

Testing robes is no easy feat. We had to strip down to our skivvies, throw on a bunch of cozy options, and, well, chill. We made note of each robe's comfort factor, which usually had to do with the material of the robe. All of the robes we featured here are sure to suit the preference of basically anyone who would ever shop for a robe, whether they want a hood, prefer something to keep them dry and warm after a shower, or just lounge in like a baller.

#6842. Melitta Baumeister Is the Designer Keeping New York Weird

The bold designer is braving the New York fashion landscape with unique shapes and high concepts.

Only at a Melitta Baumeister presentation in New York would you find the artist Kembra Pfahler playing a tuba, Paola Castro doing backflips, and Colleen Litchfield sculpting clay on the floor with sneakers gliding by on motorized platforms with chunky tires. “I really loved the idea of just doing flips in your living room,” the designer tells ELLE of her event last month. Sitting in her Greenpoint atelier in Brooklyn, Baumeister is wearing one of her signature black pointy baseball caps covered in pleated fabric. It’s become such a trademark for her that the people who know her best barely recognize her without it.

But that’s not all she’s known for. Since launching her own fashion line over a decade ago, Lady Gaga and Rihanna have worn her work, and the label has become a favorite of fashion insiders, with over-the-top conceptual shows, directional collections sold at places like Dover Street Market, and sporty collaborations. Her latest foray is a second collaboration with Nike, which involved the aforementioned performance-art-centric presentation to launch her rework of the Tabi-silhouetted Rift. Her take is a chunky, clay-inspired wedge of a shoe with gasp-inducing details like eyeball motifs and puffy logos.

Baumeister’s work has a cult following because it puts a focus on handmade details in an unusual, raw way. But she also has always gravitated towards big, voluminous shapes that take up space in an uncompromising way, with an element of sportiness. At her New York Fashion Week debut, for instance, Paralympian sprinter Scout Bassett opened the show. Sculpted dresses with bell-shaped bottoms, architectural pointed blouses, and surreally satisfying pleated dresses were put on full display with banana-shaped pouches, spiked necklaces, and, of course, that signature hat done in various colors like lemon yellow.

“I think because there’s so much out there, I feel like making statements to show creativity,” Baumeister says. “I feel like that’s why you have to push because there’s just too much boring stuff out there.” The designer describes her house codes as O lines and A lines, always with a voluminous shape. “My approach is always to make a garment kind of feel three-dimensional. There might be a drape from the side view, but it’s all very considered. It comes from hand draping, working with the fabric, and seeing what the fabric can do with its structure.”

Born in a tiny town in the Black Forest in southern Germany, Baumeister went to tailoring school at the age of 16 before studying fashion design at the Pforzheim University of Applied Sciences. She later moved to New York City to study at Parsons in the MFA Fashion Design and Society program and officially founded her line when she graduated in 2014. In 2023, she won the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund, and in 2025, she won the National Design Award for Fashion Design.

Earlier this year, the Costume Institute at the Metropolitan Museum of Art acquired her “Venus” dress and exhibited it at the “Costume Art” show. She works alongside her partner, Michal Plata, who also serves as the brand’s art director. The city continues to inspire her: “the energy is so special and so strong here that I feel like it kind of gives me that sort of harshness in design,” she says. “We’re very bold and kind of very daring. I don’t think I would do the same in Germany in my hometown.”

Though many of her pieces are designed in charcoal black, when she’s not working in neutrals, it’s neons. “I really want color to feel strong and bold rather than kind of too soft or too safe,” she says. Color is a storytelling method for her, and the brighter colors also represent energy. Baumeister continues to pull from the earliest days of her brand, like when she created clothing out of poured silicone. “I’m still very inspired by that, because it was not about caring about wearability, it was more like an art piece than clothing.” One of her brand missions is to show that garments don’t have to be traditionally sewn, or conventionally shaped. Another pillar for her is the accessories and footwear. “A bag talks so much about the character of a woman, and the shoe as well, because you can feel more feminine or more masculine or more in a certain way,” she says.

At the moment, she’s busy working on her own line (with a potential return to fashion week on her mind) after finishing her latest Nike collaboration, which just launched. The Nike collaboration includes clothing in addition to the shoes, like sculpted sweatpants accented with nose-shaped keyrings. “I always think shoes or sneakers nowadays look so much that they’re coming out of a machine and no one touched them and they’re just perfect,” she says of the collection. “I wanted to highlight that things are made by hand and there is a lot of hand work also in shoes.”

For the occasion, she actually hand-sculpted the shoes with clay in her atelier to form the final mold. That’s part of the reason why the presentation was so theatrical and involved a live sculptor: “I wanted to show how things are made. I want people to come to the thought that there’s no God-given talent, and you’re not born as a final product. Things have to be built from the ground up. There’s always another thing that you have to work on.”

That’s what makes her work so exciting. Baumeister is still most interested in what fashion can become when it refuses to conform to the typical shape.

#6840. Andy Baraghani’s New NYC Restaurant is Full of Design Surprises

“I’ve always been obsessed with design, since I was a kid,” says Andy Baraghani. “I love how restaurant interiors can take you to a different place.”

At Ditto—the all-day café he is opening in New York’s Flatiron—the chef, cookbook author, and YouTube star has given that obsession free rein. With each design decision—from the vintage glass-prism Holophane pendants in the front window to the intense blue (tinted to match Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue) of the rear dining area’s Venetian plaster walls—he asked himself: “Would I actually do this in my home?” If the answer was yes, it passed the test.

The interior of Ditto, with Venetian plaster walls in a shade matching Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue, and Model S22 chairs from Galvanitas.

For Andy Baraghani, design is something of a family affair. His husband, Keith Pollock, is a former AD editor and now a West Elm executive. But opening a restaurant was never part of the plan. In fact, when Michael Silber, a restaurant investor behind New York hot spots like Borgo, Penny, and Bistrot Ha, approached him with the idea of a laid-back restaurant open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, Baraghani admits his first reaction was: “I have no interest.”

It wasn’t for lack of experience. He had started his career in restaurants—from Chez Panisse in Berkeley, where he worked as a teenager, to Estela in New York—before becoming a food editor at Bon Appetit and winning a James Beard Award for his cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be.

But he bonded with Silber over their shared love of greenmarket cooking and decorating deep dives. When it came to Ditto, he says, he wanted the space to convey his personal style. It helped that he and Silber were on the same page. “Andy and I talked about styles ranging from Bauhaus, de Stijl, and classic modernism to 1970s and ’80s aesthetics from places like Italy and France,” Silber says.

They brought in like-minded collaborators: interior designer Eric Wink and architect Alta Indelman. Wink, a close friend of Baraghani who helped with the design of his and Pollock’s home, says the partners told him that New York’s much-missed City Bakery, which was two blocks uptown from Ditto’s 16th Street location, was an inspiration. “They wanted it to feel casual and approachable, with a bit of a New York diner quality,” Wink says.

Holophane pendant lamps hang in the restaurant’s front window.

The space, in a 1905 former factory (its last incarnation was an agnès b. store), is divided into three zones. In the front section, visitors can shop at a market area with hand-picked groceries. A glossy white counter with Bauhaus curves anchors the middle section; this is where customers line up, take a number, and either carry the food out or dine at laminate-topped tables under a trio of oversized custom fabric pendants. The menu, handwritten on a roll of butcher’s paper and updated daily, features dishes like pomegranate spoon salad and what Baraghani calls “the Platonic ideal of granola,” with tahini, maple syrup, and yogurt drizzled with fig-leaf oil.

The third zone, the one painted blue, features an open kitchen and café tables pulled up to a banquette that runs the length of the room. “There’s that good chaos in the middle and the back is a calmer moment,” says Baraghani.

Indelman, a veteran collaborator with New York restaurateurs like Andrew Tarlow and Gabe Stulman, was tasked with giving the space a utilitarian, high-tech ambience. She clad the walls and the open kitchen in patinated stainless steel and preserved industrial elements like structural arches and polished concrete floors.

But it was Baraghani and Silber who took the lead on honing the visual details of the interiors. “We went through 50 possibilities to find the right chair,” Silber says. The one they selected—a 1960s Dutch industrial chair, the Model S22 from Galvanitas—was sourced from Amsterdam Modern in Los Angeles.

Silber also spent hours on eBay bidding on midcentury ceramic bud vases. “They were each under $20 but put them together on a shelf and you have your own little Giorgio Morandi tableau,” he says.

White wall speakers and a French ceramic mask hang above the banquette, tables, and stools upholstered in Maharam’s Stripe It fabric.

The no-nonsense decor also features white wall speakers, created for the space by sound artist Tom Bloxam, and programmed with playlists created by Michael Scanlon of Chandelier Creative, which oversaw Ditto’s branding. But there are quirkier moments too. When it came to choosing fabric for the custom stools, Baraghani insisted on Maharam’s Stripe It, which he felt had a “Baja California” vibe. “We needed that twist,” he says. For his part, Wink specified his favorite stainless-steel toilet for the restrooms—Neo-Metro’s wall-mounted MiniLoo. “I added a custom wood top to soften it a bit,” Wink says.

Meanwhile, a pair of massive midcentury French ceramic faces that hang on a wall opposite the menu of the day are on loan from Baraghani’s own home. “They anchor the space and add a touch of craft,” he says. “I just knew they needed to be here.”

#6837. Jesse Jo Stark on What It Means to Be a Muse

The singer’s new Gothic country album, Muse, releases on November 6

Jesse Jo Stark wrote her latest album, Muse, in the wake of heartache. She left Los Angeles to find reprieve in the Colorado Rocky Mountains, where she found sanctuary among friends, a bottle of rosé, and a pink-halter-top-and-sweatpants combo. The melancholic album flowed out of her for three weeks, during which she transferred her emotions onto the page. “I am no longer holding on to a version of myself,” she tells Bazaar on a call from Los Angeles, on her way to a photo shoot. “There’s a freedom in moving forward.”

Stark keeps pressing on, no matter what. Outside of songwriting, she plays a key role in Chrome Hearts as the daughter of founder Richard Stark. She spent her formative years surrounded by musicians, artists, designers, and every kind of creative person imaginable, all of whom inspired her to pursue her own vision. That world endlessly inspires her to create, even when she feels low. “I’ve worn things that are absolutely horrible, and I’ve written songs that I don’t necessarily love,” she says, “but when you grow, you go back to a less constructed version of yourself.”

This more authentic version of herself fuels Muse. She shed some of the macabre edge of her debut album, 2022’s Doomed, in favor of a softer reflection on her life, love, femininity, and the natural world that inspired these songs. But above all, Stark offers a reflection on her life being put on a pedestal, a narrative that deeply considers the women in her life, from friends to her mother, Laurie Lynn Stark. This 13-track Gothic country album appropriately conveys Stark’s energy, with visuals described as “somewhat of a horror film, but I’m wearing a lace skirt.” She wrote on her Instagram, announcing the album, that the theme is “fragile but fierce femininity,” best to “enjoy with a glass of red.”

A few weeks before the release, Bazaar spoke to Stark about the women who inspired her, Napoleon’s poems to Josephine, writing songs in Colorado, and what it means to be a muse.

I was looking at a lot of mythology and history and the muses of rock ’n’ roll—women of rock ’n’ roll. If you break down the word itself, you get “used,” “amused,” “music.” I think women are admired and desired but not always heard. For me, women have this pivotal point in their life—hopefully, at one point—where they regain their strength and voice, and this album was that for me. The muse, throughout history, could also have a negative connotation and feel lonely. But I felt like putting emphasis on the reciprocity of it—then owning that and allowing it to feel beautiful. It’s a powerful word. It felt fitting for this time in my life.

There’s so much serious crossover. Being able to develop the way I feel my best on stage and design, what I wear enables me to embody that version of myself, to gather the strength to perform. Women like Daphne Guinness, Isabella Blow, and Jane Birkin have really inspired me. I’ve always wanted to not just completely mirror something from the past but re-create it as my own. I wear a loincloth on stage; it’s not that it hasn’t been done before, but the way I wear it or the way it’s designed, the accessories and tops that are paired with it... I do feel confident in me extending this already living thing but making it my own.

When I was little, I always had an attitude about the two not going hand in hand. I think that was incorrect. They’re pretty much the same expression: One’s a vocal cord and playing guitar, and the other’s a boot that you walk in.

It’s weird. My last album was highly visual. There was a lot of fantasy involved, and this is very stripped back, [both] vocal-production-wise and stylistically. I just did my first acoustic show, and I was wearing a vintage silk dress with a heel, and my hair was straight, and I had minimal makeup. Because there was such a rawness to it, especially where I recorded, which was amongst nature and very secluded. With this record, anytime I tried to put emphasis on creating a specific vibe, I rejected that.

The space and the quietness and the snow—I’ve never been one to be completely influenced by nature. I don’t love green or grass, but I love to sit in it and lie in it. I love being with animals and the snow and the sun. All these natural tones, I’m embracing the color brown like I haven’t before. It sounds so silly, but they represent a softness that I didn’t have for a while. The visuals have become somewhat of a horror film, but I’m wearing a lace skirt.

My main single from the record, “Age of Being Honest,” has been visually stimulating and powerful. I can feel every emotion through that visual. It’s rawness—in the vocals and everything. “Colorado” is the place that I literally went to and didn’t really know what was going to come from it. That set the tone for the rest of the record.

The shedding was happening as I was driving. The heartache was there, so it wasn’t difficult once I sat down to break through that human brick wall. I wanted to feel everything right away. I gotta be real, it was a white boa, a bottle of rosé, people I fuck with, the sun, and being in a really beautiful pink halter top and sweatpants half the time. I don’t think there was much going on except pain and not knowing where it was going and just sitting on the floor, living in a house with people for two weeks or a month. You can’t escape what you’re doing; I really leaned into that.

My dad had a lot to do with my love of music. I asked to play guitar at a young age. I was around a lot of rock ’n’ roll and glam—these really amazing artists who were way older than me. This desire to—and I was really shy—create something as beautiful as they had or stand as my parents could and make my own way. Music was always mine, so there was an independence to it. Finding yourself in writing, you don’t think you can write, and then you start writing poems. I loved Britney Spears. I loved the Spice Girls. But then my dad would play Merle Haggard, and he also let me listen to Christina Aguilera. I found punk rock when I was 13 because I fell in love with a punk boy. Then somehow you’re mad at everything, and you found your voice in that way. It just started to become this whole thing, and then I started singing covers because I wasn’t ready to write. And then when you write, you really write your first song. To create something out of nothing is really funny because the fact that we think we get to do that is funny to me, but also so freeing and amazing. You never want to stop.

Because good style doesn’t end in your closet.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Reformation fans have cause to rejoice today, as the beloved brand just announced its first-ever foray into home goods. This morning, Reformation launched its collaboration with French rugmaker Les Editions de Tapis.

Lauren Caris Cohan, chief creative officer at Reformation, has worked with Les Editions de Tapis for years, bringing to life rugs for Reformation stores. According to Cohan, customers have a habit of asking where the rugs are from. Now, they can bring them home for themselves.

The inspiration for the designs is rooted in French elegance and L.A. nonchalance, according to Cohan. “I think that combination is very Ref: something romantic and considered, with enough ease that it never feels precious,” she tells ELLE. “There’s a sense of humour, but it’s subtle. A rug can be a serious piece of craftsmanship and still have a cat walking across it. That balance feels very true to Reformation.”

The collection comprises nine made-to-order rugs, three of which are chintz, designed in collaboration between Cohan and Les Editions de Tapis founder Thomas Coccimiglio.

“Thomas and I have a longstanding creative partnership,” Cohan told ELLE. “Les Editions de Tapis has made exquisite rugs for our stores for nearly five years now, and we get such lovely feedback about those spaces. Bringing a special piece of that experience into our customers’ homes felt like a natural next step.”

Each rug is hand-knotted by artisans in India and Nepal. Wool, linen, and silk are featured throughout. The rugs are exclusively available online, and prices range from $1,000 to $5,000. Shop them all below and at thereformation.com.

#6824. “It’s Always About Me and What I Need or What I Want to See Out in the World”: Rick Owens on Reuniting With Adidas

“Everything I do is completely selfish,” says Rick Owens about his new Adidas collaboration, which is the latest in his off-and-on relationship with the athleticwear mega-brand. “It’s always about me and what I need or what I want to see out in the world.”

Owens is beaming in from Claridge’s hotel in London, where he was delayed because he had trouble connecting to Wi-Fi. He’s there because his longtime partner Michèle Lamy is a guest judge on RuPaul’s Drag Race. When he does appear on my screen, his face is all sharp angles framed by his signature jet-black hair parted down the middle and hanging pin straight; his nails are painted (black, of course) and on his long, equine nose is perched a pair of oversized, architectural glasses.

Owens is much like you: he suddenly knows a lot of runners. In fact, many of them are part of his “family,” a phrase he lovingly uses to describe those who work with him or are fans of the brand he’s nurtured for the better part of three decades. “So when I see them suit up and put on a branded trainer that’s not ours, it just feels like, ‘oh, we’ve got a hole.’ I mean, this is the hole that we need to fill.”

So Owens is back at it with Adidas, this time leveraging their springblade technology, a series of futuristic blades at the sole of the shoe. Owens has applied them to a gaiter-like boot and runner, and they have a characteristic futuristic, avant-garde look. “Having the opportunity to use somebody else’s technology—when they’re the best at what they do—and to be able to make runners … and to be able to get my team out of their other branded fucking sneakers and into ours, that was my motivation,” Owens said with his usual candor. “And we’re able to do it in a way that everybody can engage.”

The shoes were first revealed back in June during Owens’s runway show for the spring 2027 collection, and their dramatic, Brutalist silhouette was the perfect complement to his lean, somewhat regal ready-to-wear designs. It borrowed from his existing “Taco” series, named so as it's essentially a folded piece of fabric over the foot, yielding a deflated bag shape. “The crumpled volume feels careless and opulent at the same time,” Owens said, before adding, “at the same time, I’m half-Mexican and love tacos.”

Indeed, the shoes were just a small part of the larger Adidas collaboration, which included ready-to-wear, like sweeping hooded capes, tracksuit pants in lean and oversized silhouettes, sharp-shouldered sleeveless tunics, and jackets and bodysuits that were inflated using internal fans. The result was a mix between those blow-up Halloween costumes and what happens to Violet Beauregarde when she turns into a blueberry in Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. “I always think about how can I do a runway show that is impactful without being wasteful,” Owens said. “Without building sets that are going to be knocked down and thrown away. That’s wasteful.”

“The idea of using air and garments just fits into that,” he continued. “It’s something so pure and simple—and blending technology with something so naive, there was such charm in that. Inflated garments have been around for a long time. I mean, the Japanese workers have been using them for a long time, but then Adidas took it up, I don’t know, like 20 years ago or something. But then I found that in their archives, and so I thought, ‘Well, that’s timely.’”

And, yes, Rick-heads, those inflatable pieces will be produced for purchase. “I never wanted my runways to be an impossible dream,” he says. “In the old days, you would see runway shows with these women as these fantastic Thanksgiving Day parade floats, just these huge concoctions, and then the designer would come out at the end in jeans and a T-shirt. It deflated everything to me! It told me that the designer doesn’t believe in what he’s doing, and he’s not living it. It’s like saving your china for Sunday, or for special occasions. I want to be able to make stuff that people can have access to, and that is part of their everyday lives. So yeah, sure, there’s theater and exaggeration in what I do, but it’s connected to real life or my perception of it, which is more exaggerated than a lot of people, granted, but it’s for sale.”

While Owens is, let’s say, skeptical of the proliferation of collaborations—“If I see another collab, I’m going to roll my eyes until I fall over,” he said—the reason his with Adidas works is that they clearly give him the creative freedom to do as he pleases and it comes from a real place. It’s no big secret that Owens, with his lean physique and his at-home gym, is somewhat obsessed with working out. “When I changed my body in my 30s, when I took steroids, and started working out, it satisfied any kind of vanity the clothes would have been for. It was so much more profound than putting on an outfit. It was changing your entire bone structure. It was changing the foundation that the clothes were going to be on.”

Today his go-to gym outfit is pretty simple though—baggy shorts and thin T-shirts, and, when he’s traveling, he’ll often just wear hotel slippers. “I don’t really wear sneakers,” he says. “I’m just always in platforms.” Gym shoes, he says, take up too much room in his carry-on.

“So with Adidas, that’s my next step—to make a good workout gym shoe,” he said. “Super light and flat.”

Rick Owens for Adidas springblade shoes will range from $590 to $850 and will be available for purchase on November 17th at adidas.com, rickowens.eu, and select retailers.

#6823. All of Princess Kate’s Remembrance Sunday Looks Over the Years

The Princess of Wales first attended the event in 2011

Princess Catherine has joined the royal family for the National Service of Remembrance every year since 2011, the same year that she got married to Prince William. The somber annual ceremony, held on Remembrance Sunday at the Cenotaph, a war memorial in London, honors service members who have lost their lives at war. It takes place on the second Sunday of November, and it involves a church service, a wreath-laying ceremony, and a formal procession, all of which are attended by various members of the British royal family.

When it comes to her royal style, the Princess of Wales has long embraced a more sustainable approach, frequently rewearing dresses, jewelry, and accessories. Over the years, that style philosophy has been on full display at Remembrance Sunday, where Kate has made a tradition of recycling looks and adding sentimental touches through meaningful brooches and heirloom jewelry.

One of her signature accessories is the red poppy pin, a symbol that has come to be widely associated with the holiday. Kate is often seen wearing three poppies at once, and while the royal family has never confirmed the significance behind the number, one theory suggests it may be a personal nod to her great-grandmother’s three brothers, all of whom lost their lives during World War I.

Throughout the years, Kate has also worn pieces that once belonged to late royal family members like Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana, which she has styled with outfits from Catherine Walker, Alexander McQueen, Temperley London, Diane von Furstenberg, and more.

Ahead, take a look back at Princess Kate’s Remembrance Sunday style through the years, from her first appearance in 2011 to now. And be sure to check back for more updates once the Princess of Wales steps out for the 2026 ceremony, too.

For her first appearance with the royal family at the Cenotaph memorial, Kate wore a black Diane von Furstenberg coat adorned with a double poppy pin along with a Jane Corbett hat and Kiki McDonough earrings.

At the 2012 Remembrance Sunday ceremony, the then-Duchess of Cambridge rewore her Diane von Furstenberg coat from the previous year, this time paired with a Philip Treacy hat, Annoushka earrings, and a single sparkling poppy brooch.

Opting for a different outerwear look for her third appearance, Kate wore a single-breasted Temperley London coat, which she accessorized with a Sylvia Fletcher for Lock & Co. hat and Kiki McDonough hoop earrings with Annoushka pearl drops.

In 2014, Kate wore a black Alexander McQueen jacket over a black ruffled BCBG dress. She rewore the Jane Corbett hat she donned in 2011, and she added a floral brooch, a Mappin & Webb diamond necklace, and Princess Diana’s sapphire earrings.

Kate stepped out in another Alexander McQueen coat for the 2015 Remembrance Day service, which featured velvet trim along the collar, sleeves, and waist. The then-duchess topped it off with a Lock & Co. hat adorned with a sculptural butterfly and black veil, the Kiki McDonough hoop earrings and Annoushka pearl drops she’d worn in 2013, and a triple-poppy pin on her lapel.

In another rewear, Kate donned the same Diane von Furstenberg coat she wore to her first and second Remembrance Sunday services in 2011 and 2012. This time, she styled it with a John Boyd hat, diamond-and-pearl earrings, and three poppies on her lapel.

Kate switched up her look for the 2017 National Service of Remembrance, opting for a double-breasted, collarless Dolce & Gabbana coat with oversized gold buttons, statement Oscar de la Renta earrings in gold, and a Philip Treacy hat she wore in 2006, during her early days of dating Prince William. She also debuted a new hair look, pinning it up to create the illusion of a short bob.

The 2018 Remembrance Day Service marked a significant milestone: the 100th anniversary of the end of World War I. For the occasion, Kate wore a custom Alexander McQueen jacket with military-inspired details, including a high white collar, red shoulder embellishments, and crest-style buttons. She completed the look with a Lock & Co. hat, a triple red poppy pin, and a brooch honoring the women who served during World War I.

Opting for another military-inspired jacket, Kate wore a Catherine Walker coat and a Philip Treacy hat featuring a black veil. Forgoing her usual poppy pin, she instead wore a special pin known as the “Codebreaker’s Brooch” in honor of her grandmother who worked at Bletchley Park during World War II.

At the socially distanced 2020 Remembrance Day ceremony, held amid the COVID-19 pandemic, Kate once again opted for a military-inspired look. She wore a Catherine Walker jacket with fringe detailing at the shoulders, complete with a Philip Treacy fascinator, pearl drop earrings, and her signature triple-poppy pin.

Kate brought back her Alexander McQueen coat from the 2018 service for the 2021 Remembrance Day ceremony. She paired the repeat look with Princess Diana’s pearl earrings, a wide-brimmed Lock & Co. hat, and her signature triple-poppy pin, along with a crystal flower brooch from the Royal British Legion.

For her first Remembrance Day Service following Queen Elizabeth II’s passing, the Princess of Wales wore a black Catherine Walker coat, Princess Diana’s pearl-and-diamond earrings, and a wide-brimmed Philip Treacy hat. She completed the look with her signature trio of poppies, paired with an Art Deco-inspired diamond brooch.

The Princess of Wales opted for multiple rewears at the 2023 Remembrance Sunday service. She repeated the custom Catherine Walker coat she first wore in 2019 and the Philip Treacy hat she previously wore at the 2012 and 2017 services. Then, for some added sparkle, she wore Queen Elizabeth’s diamond-and-pearl earrings, and her signature three-poppy pin.

Kate didn’t make many public appearances in 2024 due to her cancer diagnosis, but she still attended the Remembrance Sunday service that year. She wore a Catherine Walker coat dress, featuring a velvet bow collar, and she accessorized with a Juliette Botterill hat, Queen Elizabeth’s earrings, and her triple-poppy pin.

Kate’s look at the 2025 Remembrance Sunday service featured a rewear with a new twist. She opted for the same Catherine Walker coat from 2022, but this time, she styled it with a lace navy-blue pie-crust collar blouse draping out of the top. She accessorized with a sculptural Lock & Co. fascinator, Princess Diana’s pearl-drop earrings, a single poppy brooch, and a Royal Air Force brooch.
