#6822. The Tommy Hilfiger Gifts Worth Giving

A little alpine spirit goes a long way, especially when it comes wrapped and ready to give.

Finding a great holiday gift means knowing what someone will actually love receiving—and ideally, using long after the decorations come down. For the friend who looks forward to a weekend in the mountains, that might mean a cozy knit or a warm accessory. For the frequent traveler, a polished wallet or a toiletry bag could be just the thing. And sometimes, a little fragrance is all it takes to make a gift feel special.

Tommy Hilfiger has been putting its own spin on American classics since 1985, drawing on the easy confidence of East Coast prep and the sporty influences that have long defined its look. This heritage feels right at home in the brand’s alpine campaign, where familiar staples take on a winter-ready appeal. The result is a gift selection that moves from cozy cold-weather favorites to thoughtful little luxuries, with plenty of Tommy’s signature style.

A cable-knit sweater is a gift she’ll reach for all winter. This lightweight cotton version has a relaxed, easy fit, classic crew neck, and ribbed trim. The traditional knit gives it a timeless appeal, while the soft pink shade adds a fresh touch. It’s an easy choice for everything from a weekend in the mountains to a casual day around town.

For the friend who always feels a chill, this knit hood is a fun alternative to the usual winter hat. The design features a monogram logo for a signature touch and offers extra coverage for cold-weather walks, snowy weekends, and everything in between.

Gloves are easy to overlook when shopping for gifts, which makes a good pair all the more welcome. This wool-blend knit version is a gift with staying power, adding a classic finishing touch to a cold-weather look. Tuck them into a gift box for someone planning a mountain escape, or give them to the friend who never leaves home without checking the temperature first.

This trifold wallet gets its personality from a buckle accent and monogram detail, giving the compact design a polished finish. It’s a nice option for someone who likes a bit of branding without carrying a logo-heavy bag, and its smaller profile makes room for the rest of the essentials.

There’s something especially nice about unwrapping a new fragrance during the holidays. Tommy Hilfiger’s Freedom comes in a generous 3.4-ounce bottle, making it a gift with staying power.

This monogram-print toiletry bag from Tommy Hilfiger gives skin care, makeup, and other travel necessities a dedicated place, while the allover pattern makes it easy to spot in an overstuffed suitcase. Consider it a small upgrade for the friend who always has another trip in mind.

#6819. Bangladesh Factories Grind to a Halt Amid Wage Protests. What’s Next?

The Mirpur area of Bangladesh’s capital, Dhaka, is usually a hive of activity. One of the country’s five major manufacturing hubs, it is home to more than 300 garment factories, making clothes for global brands and retailers including Walmart, H&M, Zara, Levi’s, Marks & Spencer and Primark. But on Thursday, the last working day of the week in Bangladesh, the area was eerily quiet.

The calm comes after a stormy week, which saw workers take to the streets to protest the national minimum wage, demanding the formation of a government-led Minimum Wage Board and a substantial raise from BDT 12,500 (around $100) to BDT 30,000 (around $240) per month. On November 2, more than 600 of the country’s 4,000 garment factories were forced to suspend operations for the day due to protests. By Tuesday, one worker had been killed in Gazipur, another major industrial hub, as law enforcement agencies moved to contain the unrest, which had spread across major garment manufacturing centers, disrupting factory operations and traffic. Police say more than 100 people were arrested. And by Wednesday, there was a slight reprieve: protests temporarily subsided as the government announced a Minimum Wage Board, and declared that a revised minimum wage structure for garment workers will take effect in December, with higher payments reflected in January payslips.

While the Minimum Wage Board is unlikely to meet protestors’ BDT 30,000 demands ($240), its formation is seen as a major step forward. Wage structure for garment workers hasn’t changed since 2023. “We can say our first demand has been met, as a wage board has been formed and they said that the new wage will take effect in December,” says Sajal Sardar, a sewing machine operator at a knitwear factory in Mirpur. Sardar is one of around four million garment workers in Bangladesh, more than half of whom are women. Despite serving as a cornerstone of the national economy, these workers continue to live in difficult conditions.

Minimum wage protests in Bangladesh – and the response from police – have caused significant disruption in key garment making districts.

A decade ago, 23-year-old Sardar started working in factories as a child. During that time, he has been unable to build up any savings, as the minimum wage is so scant. He belongs to a family of seven, in which he and his brother are the only earners, bringing home a combined monthly income of around BDT 30,000. He personally earns BDT 14,200 ($115) of that — or BDT 17,000-18,000 ($136-144) with overtime. At times, the family is forced to borrow money to meet unexpected expenses, such as medical costs and younger siblings’ tuition fees.

Like many of the workers involved, Sardar sees protesting as a last resort, prompted by years of unmet government promises and rising living costs. “We don’t want to take to the streets,” he says, “but there is no affordable healthcare for us. Landlords keep raising house rents every January. The prices of staple food items and cooking gas have gone up several times during this period, and our wages have remained the same.”

The latest round of protests follow intense clashes throughout 2023, after which the former Bangladeshi dictator Sheikh Hasina was ousted in a student-led popular uprising. An interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus took office in 2024, and was replaced by the current government following elections in February 2026. When Yunus was installed, the new government introduced a legal requirement to form a wage board that would review minimum wages every three years, replacing the previous five-year interval. But progress has been slower than expected. “The government should have initiated the process by forming the wage board six months before the ending of the three-year tenure,” says Sardar.

Experts say the aftershocks of the protests will be felt across the garment industry for years to come.

Unions support the decision to determine a new minimum wage in December, says Khairul Mamun Mintu, a union leader at the Bangladesh Garment Workers Trade Union Center. But if the proposed restructure fails to meet protestors’ demands, the fight will continue. “We have placed our demands. Now, stakeholders will decide what would be a reasonable wage for all. “If that also doesn’t work, we will have to take to the streets again.”

It’s been a difficult few years for Bangladesh’s economy, casting considerable doubt over whether the proposed minimum monthly wage of BDT 30,000 ($240) is achievable. Although the country’s export earnings rose 6% to $17.04 billion in the third quarter, the trade deficit widened by 31% year-on-year to $7.48 billion, as the war in the Middle East sent its fuel import bill soaring. The new Minimum Wage Board will need to balance these considerations with workers’ demands.

Projections by independent institutions also point to mounting economic challenges. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has lowered its growth forecast for Bangladesh for the current year to 4%, while projecting inflation at 9% (experts warn that the actual rate could be as high as 20%). Meanwhile, the World Bank has also sharply downgraded Bangladesh’s growth forecast for the 2026-27 full year to 3.4%, down from 4.6% in June and 6.1% in January.

This downward spiral has hit fashion manufacturing hard. The new government, led by Tarique Rahman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which assumed office following the February 12 election, has raised fuel prices twice, in April and September, resulting in a cumulative increase of more than 35%. And electricity prices at the retail level also rose by more than 16% in June. Meanwhile, retail Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) prices have increased in two consecutive hikes over the past two months, climbing from BDT 1,625 ($13) to BDT 2,060 ($16) per 12 kilogram cylinder. In March, the same cylinder cost BDT 1,340 ($10).

All of this means fashion manufacturers are grappling with a tight squeeze on prices, even before potential wage increases come into play. If brands aren’t willing to pay more to accommodate these cost hikes, it’s likely that workers will bear the brunt.

The latest wave of protests has caused substantial losses for factory owners, who manufacture clothes for global fashion brands at relatively low prices. ABM Shamsuddin, a factory owner who represents manufacturers on the newly formed six-member wage board, said the unrest has caused shipment losses worth BDT 850 million (around $68.3 million).

International buyers tend to pursue three options in these circumstances, he says. Ideally, they would accept delayed shipments without imposing penalties, but more likely they will demand that products be delivered at a 50% discount, or ask factories to send the shipments by air rather than sea shipping. Either choice would be a significant financial hit for the factory owner. Instead, he hopes global brands acknowledge that the unrest was beyond factory owners’ control. “They can see what is happening here.”

The Clean Clothes Campaign (CCC), a global network of labor unions and non-governmental organizations, is urging global fashion brands sourcing from Bangladesh to support garment workers’ demands. Ideally, brands would also publicly commit to continue sourcing from Bangladesh and ring-fence labor costs, or offer commercial terms that would enable suppliers to pay the new minimum wage, reassuring the government and employers that higher wages would not drive production to other countries. “It is crucial that brands act immediately and speak out in support of workers’ demands rather than waiting until the wage negotiations are over,” the organization’s living wage coordinator Anne Bienias said in a statement.

According to Mahmud Hasan Khan, president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), the apex body representing garment manufacturers, protests tend to erupt whenever the time comes to revise workers’ wages. Such persistent unrest has undermined international buyers’ confidence in Bangladeshi manufacturers, but angst is misdirected toward protestors and factories. “They (the buyers) can convey their concerns to the government in writing,” says Khan. “Both their interests and ours are at stake.”

The bigger issue is the lack of collective bargaining mechanisms inside factories, adds Kalpona Akter, president of the Bangladesh Garment and Industrial Workers Federation (BGIWF). “If workers could negotiate directly with factory owners inside the factories, they wouldn’t have to take to the streets,” she says. Often, by the time the government has reviewed wages and made incremental changes, progress is obsolete, she adds, pointing to the interim government’s previous attempt to raise the annual wage increment for garment workers from 5% to 9%. “Since the basic salary is quite low, the increment does not make much difference. Commodity prices rise at a pace that wages cannot keep up with.”

Union leaders say that while manufacturers and the government are responsible for ensuring workers’ welfare, international buyers also have a share of the responsibility. A report published in May by the CCC and Public Eye found that global fashion brands were paying almost the same prices per item as they did 20 years ago, with some prices even 30% lower in inflation-adjusted terms. This, the report said, “undermines suppliers’ economic resilience and depresses wages”, adding that buyers still source a standard cotton T-shirt for around $2-3 per piece, with some paying as little as $1.

This race to the bottom is compounded by the country’s low labor costs, says Akter: “[Brands] enjoy the bigger piece of the pie here.”

Moving forward, Akter says manufacturers should first increase workers’ wages and then negotiate with buyers to ensure that the additional costs are reflected in purchasing prices. “Otherwise, buyers will stand firm on their position, manufacturers will keep bleeding, and workers will keep protesting on the streets.”

#6814. From Your Wardrobe to Your Living Room: Reformation Debuts Its First Rug Collection

What makes a good outfit? Some would argue it’s all about an excellent accessory; others, the perfect white tee. And in the home? Well, ask an interiors expert, and many would argue it’s all about a great rug. For those who take as much pleasure in dressing their homes as they do themselves, Reformation’s new collaboration with luxury rug brand Les Éditions de Tapis—out today—is well worth a look.

Designed by Thomas Coccimiglio, founder and creative director of Les Éditions de Tapis, and Lauren Caris Cohan, Reformation’s chief creative officer, the limited-edition collection comprises nine rugs, with hand-drawn designs featuring everything from tigers and swans to palm trees. Playful, characterful, and just the right side of eccentric, they’re the sort of pieces that would look just as at home in a lofty city apartment as they would in a cozy country cottage.

The pair describe the collection as “Parisian elegance meets LA nonchalance.” Says Coccimiglio, “I’ve always been fascinated by the romanticized visions that French and American cultures have of one another. Americans dream of French history, Versailles, and the grandeur of the 18th century, while we French have our own fantasy of Los Angeles as a city of endless possibilities, rock ‘n’ roll, cinema, and glamour.”

The collection, he explains, is an expression of this cultural exchange, marrying sophistication with humor and a healthy dose of the unexpected—an approach that chimes rather nicely with Reformation’s own “effortless and witty” brand identity.

It’s a creative partnership that has been brewing for some time. Coccimiglio and Cohan have worked together on the rugs in Reformation’s stores for the past five years, helping bring the brand's aesthetic to life beyond the clothes. “Thomas has a similar sense of humor to us, and we've been able to inject that into the storytelling through the rugs in our stores, which are exquisite,” explains Cohan, who oversees the design of Reformation’s retail spaces.

The rugs have become something of a talking point among customers, many of whom have asked where they can buy them for their own homes. So, creating a collection they could actually take home felt like a natural next step.

Cohan gave Coccimiglio (almost) free rein to bring his vision to life. “With all our collaborations, we choose partners we trust, whether that’s Alexa Chung or Camille Rowe. We steer the ship, but we know we get the best out of people that way,” she says. “Thomas designed every single element of these rugs.”

Her only stipulation? That the designs incorporate shades from Reformation’s Holiday collection, which has been photographed against the rugs for the accompanying campaign. A neat meeting of the brand’s fashion and interiors worlds.

While Cohan’s favorite piece is the Très Grand Chintz Rug in Dark Wine, Coccimiglio namechecks the Swans Fans Rug in French Blue, which (true to its name) features two swans. “Swans belong to the romantic imagery of French châteaux, gliding across ornamental lakes and gardens,” he explains of the design, which began life as a sketch on a Post-it note. “I started imagining their tails as delicate, fan-shaped feathers, almost like the elaborate hand fans from the 18th century—I loved the idea of transforming two romantic swans into something a little more decorative and Art Deco.”

Hand-knotted by artisans in India and Nepal using wool, linen, and silk, these rugs aren’t just pretty to look at—they’re made to last. But when it comes to styling one at home, should a rug be the star of the show or more of a supporting act?

“I always start with the rug, then build a room around it,” says Cohan, who also finds time to work on residential interiors outside of Reformation. “It can be a statement piece with everything else kept sparse, or you can layer on top of it.” Her biggest piece of advice? Don’t skimp on size. A rug that’s too small can throw off the proportions of an otherwise beautiful room.

For Coccimiglio, a rug grounds a room, bringing together the furniture, objects, and, most importantly, the people who inhabit it. “There’s a beautiful thought that is often attributed to Edgar Allan Poe—the soul of the apartment is the carpet,” he says. “And I couldn’t agree more.”

#6809. Rihanna Borrows a Fresh Styling Trick From the Runways

Stars, they’re just like us: they even go to the mall! This weekend, Rihanna hit up The Grove in Los Angeles, where she was spotted shopping up a storm. (Maybe she was getting a head start on securing holiday gifts for the family.) And as we’ve come to expect, the star wasn’t shuffling around in athleisure, but flexing a full statement look for the outing. I mean, is it even a Rihanna spotting without her serving up an outfit that we want to instantly replicate?

Her latest off-duty look, however, was not about the actual designer pieces that she was wearing—rather, how she wore them. Sure, her classic khaki trench coat, monogrammed Louis Vuitton bag, and suede Miu Miu x New Balance sneakers were all striking enough on their own, but it was more so her styling approach to them that really sealed the deal. And better yet, she borrowed a styling flourish we’ve clocked on the recent runways, one that’s super easy to replicate.

Her effortlessly-cool outfit formula? It all lies in the half-tucked shirt collar. By popping out just one side of her classic white shirt’s collar, the ensemble instantly felt just a little more undone, a little more happenstance—a little less perfect or trying too hard. Adding the slightly off-kilter touch to an outfit is a move we’ve seen done in countless runway shows this season, including in the fall collections of Bottega Veneta, Celine, Balenciaga, and Jil Sander (to name a few).

The question is: do we think Rihanna intentionally replicated the new, catwalk-approved way to wear a shirt, or does she just dress that flawlessly naturally? Even the way she carried her LV bag—by her hip, more like a clutch—was very reminiscent of the way models carry them during high-fashion shows. But Rihanna doesn’t need a stage. . . The streets are her runway.

#6804. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley Wears the Backless Dress to End All Backless Dresses

Every so often, a moment in the middle of the fashion month marathon makes even the weariest editors sit up a little straighter in their seats. This season, it came courtesy of Demna, whose spring 2027 show featured a formidable cast of characters, from sultry sirens in sequins to coiffured OAPs to rich-bitch equestrians. Joining this crew was Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, in an enormous faux-fur coat and sunglasses, looking like the kind of woman who knows her way around a prenup.

Catching up ahead of the LACMA gala this weekend, the star confirmed that our new favorite leading lady is still very much in the room. “She’s back,” Huntington-Whiteley tells me, albeit wearing slightly less clothing this time around. She swapped the enrobing coat for an ostensibly demure high-necked black dress that’s more of a barely-there number at the back. “It’s very Demna-coded, and I think there’s definitely something very similar in spirit to the character,” she says.

The characters, Rosie explains, were divided into three archetypes: “The rebellious aristocrat, the snob and the eccentric. I actually felt like my character embodied a little of all three. There was something obviously very commanding and unapologetic about her, with a certain sort of eccentricity and attitude. I also love that she didn’t take herself too seriously.” It seems the transformation was convincing enough for Derek Blasberg to tell her, “I can see you dug really deep for this character.”

Rosie’s trip into the Demna-verse served as a reminder that a little theatrics can go a long way. “My job as a model is basically being able to step into different characters and explore a designer’s vision. It’s about really understanding their world and finding a way to bring that character to life that feels authentic and natural to me,” she says, adding: “It’s always a reminder, when you do projects like this, of how important attitude is with the clothes we embody. Ultimately, clothes are clothes, but the way you wear them, the attitude and the way you embody them are what really make something memorable, what makes something iconic.”

Rosie’s earliest memories of Gucci are firmly rooted in the Tom Ford era. “Of course, back then I could never afford Gucci, but what’s always struck me is that the brand has this glamour to it. It’s unapologetic,” she says. Those campaigns, she remembers, were everywhere when she was starting out, “at a time when fashion imagery felt like something you really studied and committed to memory. They become part of your reference bank, so to speak. I loved that era and always will. I’ve really worn and loved Gucci on the red carpet ever since, and certainly in my real life too.”

Wearing Gucci at the LACMA Art+Film Gala in 2012.

As for her favourite Gucci looks over the years, a few spring to mind. Currently taking the crown (aside from this weekend’s LACMA look, of course) was her 2012 LACMA appearance, for which she wore another open back number, this time in green. “It was sharp and clean, but really sexy.” Clearly, Rosie and Gucci have had a few good outings together, and if Demna has anything to do with it, there are probably a few more characters still to come.

#6803. All the Celebrity Looks From the 2026 LACMA Art+Film Gala

Every year, the art, film, fashion, and entertainment industries head to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) for an evening of glamorous fundraising, celebration, and live music. The Art+Film Gala, as it’s called, has seen everyone from Kim Kardashian and Kendall Jenner to Charli XCX and Troye Sivan to Cindy Crawford and Kaia Gerber, welcoming models, actors, philanthropists, musicians, athletes, and more.

Since its inaugural edition back in 2011, the star-studded event has supported the museum’s efforts to expand its programming, making film more central to its exhibitions and education. With sponsorship from Gucci, it has placed a focus on the intersection of art and film, honoring painters, cinematographers, and directors alike for their global contributions. Tonight, it recognized the work of Vija Celmins, known for her photo-realistic paintings exploring the complexity of nature, and Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve. Blackpink’s Rosé was tapped for an intimate performance, and, for the 15th year, Leonardo DiCaprio and LACMA trustee Eva Chow were appointed co-chairs.

As for the guests, Chris Burden’s public Urban Light installation—a collection of oversize street lamps that doubled as a red carpet for the evening—saw the likes of Alex Consani, Nicole Kidman, Kylie Jenner, and Paris Hilton. The familiar faces were joined by Anya Taylor-Joy, Alix Earle, Andrew Garfield, Benito Skinner, Candice Swanepoel, Chloe Kim, Emily Ratajkowski, Jordyn Woods-Towns, Julia Garner, Lindsey Vonn, Monica Lewinsky, Odessa A’zion, Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Salma Hayek, Viola Davis, and more.

#6798. Studio Visit: The Unassuming Chinatown Space Where Zane Li Has Built an Award-Winning Brand

Behind designer Zane Li’s desk is an oversized whiteboard with every look from his spring 2027 collection neatly pinned up in orderly rows. “Every time I start a new collection, I always put the past collection behind me because I want to have an extension of ideas from the past season, and then see what we can do new,” he says. “Especially right now, we’re at the kind of inspiration-gathering and silhouette-designing phase.”

We’re at the Chinatown office and studio for his label Lii, located along a particularly trendy stretch of dingy Canal Street. It’s a surprisingly small, modest space considering how much the 26-year-old Li has captured the attention of the fashion industry in the three short years he’s been running his business. Just this year, he has taken home both the LVMH Karl Lagerfeld Prize for Innovation and the top honor at the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund, and was also nominated for the CFDA Award for Emerging Designer of the Year.

Across from Li’s desk, industrial racks filled with past seasons’ designs.

The third-floor space is essentially a small white-walled square with high ceilings and three windows looking onto a balcony that faces an interior airshaft. On one wall is a vintage-style sink, and at the center of the room is a Donald Judd-ish birch table from the popular furniture shop Lichen in Ridgewood, Brooklyn. Directly across is a floor-to-ceiling industrial rod set-up stuffed with brightly-colored samples, some in plastic coverings.

Li’s desk is spare and tidy—an orange stapler and tape dispenser, a blue square of Post-Its, a paper cup of coffee, and a rectangular box of Chinese cigarettes. In some ways, it evokes his own work—familiar American sportswear shapes distilled into geometric forms and rendered in cheery Crayola hues of pink, red, powder blue, and kelly green. “Lii is about making familiar things unfamiliar, in a certain way—through fabrics, through colors,” Li says. “We want to take certain shapes into people’s real life and keep the volume, keep the look, but make the garment practical and make it accessible for the wearer.”

Art and photography are frequent starting points, and next to his desk is a baker’s rack stuffed with thick picture books. Not far from his laptop are photo printouts and a binder filled with fabrics. “We’re trying to see what kind of combo or what kind of formula looks good visually,” he says. “And from there I’ll start patterning, I’ll start designing, which is a personal and abstract process, I will say, because it’s not really ... I try not to start a collection from a garment. I kind of always try to start collections from either a piece of Ellsworth Kelly work, a piece of installation art, a Balenciaga gown.”

Li’s CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund and LVMH Karl Lagerfeld prize on a shelf.

Art and design books near Li’s desk are sources of inspiration.

Li lives just a few blocks away—he measures the time it takes for him to get from the studio to his home not in distance or in traditional markers of time, but in “half-ciggies.” “I can’t even finish a cigarette walking from here to my apartment,” he says. He splits his time between here, where the clothes are designed; China, where they are manufactured; and Paris, where his press and sales teams are located. He starts his days around 9 or 10 am, grabbing orange juice at the deli downstairs to drink while checking emails and dealing with urgent press or sales matters. Then he’ll go out and get lunch from a local spot, grab a coffee, and start the design part of his day, which often can stretch to 2 am, to stay in touch with his partners in China.

Li pulls a Rineke Dijkstra book of photography from his crowded shelf as an example of a source of inspiration he returns to. “Her narrative about people, about what you can see from an image, and what their moods and emotions are, is really strong,” he says. “And I tend to want my garment, my design or idea, to evoke the same feeling. So, sometimes if I feel bored or if I don’t feel like what I want to do, then I’ll look at this book, and it gives me an instant hit—and then we’ll start from there.”

Printouts or art and archival fashion serve as inspiration.

Zane has a board from the previous season set up behind his desk to help him work on the season ahead.

Li pulls off a three-tiered, asymmetrical skirt made from a spongy scuba fabric as an example of a recent design he’s particularly proud of. “It’s quite comfortable to wear, but, also, has this supportive shape thanks to the fabric. And we just decided to make a paneled skirt with darts that’s feminine, but I think the material made it look sporty as well.” He also pulls out an oversized, color-blocked polo shirt with hanging fabric off the sleeves. “We always try to explore ideas of a T-shirt because we feel like this is something so practical and so easy, but there’s a lot of possibilities in it,” he says. “I like the shape and having a graphic-ness on the body. We tested 10 different prototypes—about what kind of proportion, how long the strings should be to make the garment look balanced, and so on. It’s kind of fun. It’s kind of like you’re drawing squares or drawing just circles on the paper, and you’re trying to find the perfect, the most balanced circle on the paper.”

“It’s kind of like the practice of that,” he continued. “Which is really flat, and I really enjoy the transformation from that flat pattern into something that people wear on the body, and feels quite three-dimensional.”

It’s a marvel to think that Li has built so much from such a small space in such a short time. Currently, he is the only full-time employee—his husband, the stylist Jason Rider, is heavily involved but has his own career, while his studio and production managers are still freelance. Li says he plans to use the winnings from his recent prizes to help build out a more robust team. There is one silent team member keeping watch in the corner: a dummy mannequin, usually used for draping. Li mostly designs on his computer, so she’s more of a mascot. “She’s my good luck charm,” Li says, giving her a hug. “She brings me comfort.”

#6794. Here’s Your First Look at the Broadway Cast of ‘Paddington: The Musical’

Hold on to your hats (and your little blue toggle coats): Paddington is New York City-bound.

Next year, the multiple-Olivier Award-winning theatrical sensation that is Paddington: The Musical opens at the Al Hirschfeld Theatre on Broadway—bringing with it, yes, the four-foot-tall puppet that is Paddington Bear himself, but also a wonderfully star-studded cast.

Performers in the New York production will include Kelvin Dukes as Tony, Drew Gehling (Waitress) as Mr. Brown, Allison Guinn (Operation Mincemeat) as Lady Sloane, Tony Hale (Veep, Arrested Development) as Mr. Curry, J. Quinton Johnson (Hamilton) as Grant, Leslie Rodriguez Kritzer (The Fantasticks) as Millicent Clyde, Zonya Love (The Color Purple) as Tanya, Serena Parrish (Don’t Say Good Luck) as Judy Brown, Karen Ziemba (Contact) as Mrs. Bird, Chip Zien (Into the Woods) as Mr. Gruber, and, as Mrs. Brown, one Jessie Mueller (Waitress, Carousel), making her first appearance on Broadway since starring in Tracy Letts’s The Minutes in 2022.

Additionally, Arti Shah and James Hameed, who brought Paddington Bear to life onstage in the West End, will reprise their joint role at the Hirschfeld.

“This just felt like the right show, with the right message,” Mueller tells Vogue of her grand return to the Main Stem. “Paddington is a character I’ve known and loved all my life! And I’m so excited to be back on Broadway to share this story of love, family, kindness and inclusion.”

“I really hope the Broadway audience can find a place in their hearts to look after this bear,” says the show’s composer, Tom Fletcher. (Paddington’s book has been adapted by Jessica Swale, and Luke Sheppard directs.) “Writing the songs for Paddington: The Musical has been the greatest honor of my life, and it goes without saying that getting to bring our show to New York is an actual dream come true.”

He goes on: “The importance of kindness is at the heart of our story in London, and I hope we can bring that message to New York and spread kindness like marmalade.”

New Yorkers should be on the lookout for a polite little bear from Peru in the spring: Previews of Paddington: The Musical begin on Tuesday, March 30, with an opening night set for Sunday, April 18.

#6790. After a Devastating Fire, This South Australia Lodge Has Returned as One of the World’s Wildest, Most Wonderful Stays

The first thing you’ll notice while driving across Kangaroo Island is the trees. More specifically, their strange, topsy-turvy appearance: blackened, skeletal eucalyptus trunks that sprout lime-green foliage from about halfway up. As you get closer to the southern edge of the island, where the land falls away into the roiling waters—the final frontier of the inhabited world before Antarctica—the foliage becomes increasingly flattened and twisted, whipped by the unrelenting Southern Ocean winds. Pulling into a set of pale, discreet limestone gates and up a series of long, winding roads that serve as a driveway, you might even spot the charred branches’ fresh leaves glowing almost neon in the afternoon light.

And then, it appears: a sinuous, low-slung ribbon of limestone and glass hugging the clifftop, an architectural marvel that shines like a beacon above the scrubby, sun-bleached coast. At last, you’ve made it all the way to Southern Ocean Lodge.

No matter where you’re traveling from, it’s an undertaking to get here (though it will become a little easier once Qantas launches its direct New York to Sydney flights in 2028). But from the very first glimpse, you’ll sense it was all worth it—not only is Southern Ocean Lodge one of the world’s most epic and spectacularly situated hotels, but it’s also a symbol of extraordinary resilience. When the catastrophic Black Summer bushfires tore across Kangaroo Island in January 2020, the original lodge—first built in 2008, and widely considered the crown jewel of Australian luxury tourism—was reduced to ash in a matter of hours. For founders James and Hayley Baillie, the husband-and-wife duo behind the property, walking among the ruins was understandably devastating. But they quickly decided the hotel must have a second act. The original architect, Max Pritchard, went back to the drawing board to reimagine the property from the ground up, refining its footprint to embed it even more deeply into its surroundings, and in late 2023, it finally reopened—sleeker, tougher, and somehow even more breathtaking than before.

What changed? The angles, for one. Pritchard reoriented the entire 25-suite building slightly to the southwest, ensuring every curved glass pavilion now frames the uninterrupted drama of Hanson Bay’s rugged headlands. A subtle tweak on paper, but in practice, it’s a revelation: morning light now falls even deeper into the living spaces, and the vast blue skies and white surf crashing against the bluffs are a permanent, constantly shifting wallpaper. The spa was moved into its own pavilion, and a four-bedroom compound with its own infinity pool was added just above the hotel’s central hub. Perhaps most importantly, the retreat is now an off-grid fortress and engineered to the highest-tier bushfire standards, ensuring it’s ready to endure whatever Mother Nature throws at it next.

On the balmy day I arrived in late spring, the scene was altogether more calm: a light sea breeze barely ruffled the coastal mallee. Stepping into the Great Room, the lodge’s communal heart, the ceiling seems to hover weightlessly, and the panoramic, floor-to-ceiling glass walls curve around like the cockpit of a spaceship. There, my travel companion (in fact, my mom) and I were handed welcome glasses of Adelaide Hills sparkling and canapés—crisp seed crackers topped with crushed avocado and golden arancini crowned with a cloud of shaved cheese—then ushered directly toward the view of rolling green and gold headlands drifting down into a crescent of pristine white sand stretching as far as the eye can see. There was no formal check-in process, as all of that had been done even before arrival, and nearly everything here—the food, the experiences, and even the cellar full of curated South Australian wines—is included in the nightly rate. Sitting beside the suspended, Jetsons-esque fireplace with a cocktail in hand as sea eagles circle outside, the already whisper-thin threshold between the serene, glass-walled sanctuary of the resort and the untamed wilderness beyond seemed to dissipate entirely.

The effect in the rooms was similar: we were guided down the curved, light-dappled corridor to a Flinders Suite—after the intrepid British navigator Matthew Flinders, who charted (and named) Kangaroo Island in 1802—where the floor plan steps down into a glass-wrapped sunken lounge designed to feel as if it’s floating above the coastline. At three in the afternoon, the space was still lit with honeyed sunshine, picking out the crisp oatmeal and fresh ocean blues of the interiors, while a small fireplace crackled away on the far wall. And as the afternoon melted into evening, the mood had mellowed even further. The stark white clifftops in the distance warmed to a shade of amber, casting long shadows across the dunes. By the time we were getting dressed for dinner, the horizon was deep, bruised pink, and, stepping outside, you could just about see the Southern Cross constellation sparkling in the twilight sky.

As for that dinner? Every meal here a masterclass in hyper-local dining. (Anyone who’s been to Australia already knows how universally excellent the food is across the board—so for something to dazzle at this level takes serious culinary chops.) Meals revolve around whatever has arrived from island producers that morning—when I was there, that included sweet Kangaroo Island marron from local purveyor Scott Wilson, silky confit king salmon, and handmade orecchiette tossed with fennel-spiked pork and garden peas. (Naturally, I felt it was my journalistic duty to try both mains.) Sitting in the candlelit dining room as the dark fully swallowed the headlands—and even with guests seated at different tables—the room had the warm, convivial feeling of a private dinner party. Then again, that was probably also helped by the fact that, should you so wish, every dish can arrive accompanied by unpretentious pairings from that encyclopedic wine list, which runs the gamut from crisp coastal whites to velvety reds from vineyards on the island itself.

Somehow, I’ve got this far without even mentioning the wildlife—that’s primarily why people come to Kangaroo Island, after all. (Clue’s in the name, I suppose.) Even on the drive over, after our up-and-down 30-minute prop flight from Adelaide, we spotted wallabies hopping through the scrub and clusters of Kangaroo Island kangaroos through the ramshackle roadside fences; simply lazing around the lodge itself presents plenty of opportunities to watch ospreys soar past the windows, or to use the provided binoculars in your room to keep watch for pods of dolphins carving through the breaks below.

The real highlights, though, are the daily excursions led by the lodge’s team of in-house naturalists. They rotate shifts between guiding drives and sharing local lore at dinner, and many are in their 20s and 30s, here on three- to six-month seasonal residencies, ensuring they’re still as excited by it all as you are. Don’t let those fresh faces fool you, however: almost all of them are either studying for (or already hold) degrees in environmental science, marine biology, or conservation, and they carry that formidable academic depth with classic Aussie irreverence. Our guide on two afternoons, Angela, could break down the exact timeline of the post-bushfire regenerative cycle, yet introduced a sprawling colony of Australian sea lions by noting that their daily routine of sleeping 20 hours and sunning themselves on the sand was “basically me on my days off.”

On the subject of those sea lions: The following morning, Angela took us and a few fellow guests 40 minutes or so away in a minivan and down onto the wide, windswept beaches of Seal Bay, where we were able to walk (albeit slowly and quietly) just yards from dozens of wild sea lions. Some were dozing in tangled pairs right in the dune grass, while another sat upright like a whiskered Buddha, tilting its snout toward the salty surf spray. Upon walking to the water’s edge, one curious pup swam right over to me and surfaced just a few feet away, before somersaulting back beneath the waves—pure magic.

Later, venturing inland into the gums to the Hanson Bay Wildlife Sanctuary, the wildlife safari continued with a stroll through the eucalyptus forests, where we spotted a solitary koala wedged asleep in the crook of a high fork in the branches; upon stepping out into the wide-open pastures, we wandered through packs of kangaroos bounding solo across open ground, nibbling at tall she-oak branches, and heading to the shaded undergrowth to nurse their little joeys.

The most breathtaking visit of all, however, was the afternoon out that came billed as Wonders of Kangaroo Island. Wondrous, indeed: Over three and a half hours traversing Flinders Chase National Park on the island’s rugged western tip, the weather took on a moody, cinematic flavor as the skies turned steel gray and the Southern Ocean grew especially tempestuous. First up was a visit to Admirals Arch, where a timber boardwalk snakes down through the coastal heath toward the sea. Descending into the enormous limestone grotto, where jagged stalactites hung like giant teeth, we could hear a mysterious chorus of asthmatic grunts and wheezes; peering through veils of salty sea-mist, we discovered it was the barking of half a dozen raucous long-nosed fur seals, slipping and sliding around the slick rock ledges and tidepools.

Then, we paid a visit to the delightfully named Remarkable Rocks: a group of colossal smooth granite boulders, appearing from the far distance like a mythical sea monster that’s washed ashore. Up close, it’s more like a surrealist sculpture park, 500 million years in the making. Hollowed out by centuries of wind and sea into fantastical, wave-like shapes, the rocks perch precariously on the edge of the abyss, their weathered gray surfaces splashed with rust-like orange lichen. As the gale-force winds whipped so hard you could lean forward into the gusts and still remain upright, with nothing between us and the endless emptiness of the Antarctic on the other side, it was impossible not to feel small, even insignificant. It was strangely comforting.

Back at the lodge that evening, after a long, luxurious bath, it was time for another slap-up meal—seared beef carpaccio with pickled shallots, followed by pan-roasted barramundi over braised Asian greens, crowned with a nest of crispy enoki. (All washed down with a yuzu mocktail for me and a velvety local Shiraz for my mom.) On the way back to the room, I paused before a delicate, quiet installation along the hallway wall. Mounted against the smooth plaster were fragments of melted glass, charred stone, and shattered pottery gathered directly from the ashes of the original property after the catastrophic 2020 fires. The work is titled Relics, and was created by local Kangaroo Island artist Janine Mackintosh; as the placard accompanying it noted, Mackintosh didn’t want the piece to feel grim, but rather a joyful tribute to the lodge that stood here first.

There was plenty of heartache and hand-wringing after the devastation wrought by the fires, to be sure—and one imagines there were several moments when the Baillies doubted it would even be possible to recreate the singular alchemy of this place. Thank goodness they did. Really, there could be no greater testament to the indomitable spirit and grit of this island community than bringing its crown jewel, Southern Ocean Lodge, back—perhaps not bigger, but undoubtedly better than ever before.

#6789. Kim Kardashian Returns to the LACMA Gala in Burgundy Gucci Sequins

Her turtleneck dress dipped dangerously low in the back

Kim Kardashian is back at the LACMA Art+Film Gala. A frequent staple of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s annual fundraising event, the reality star returned to the famed street-lamp installation (Chris Burden’s Urban Light) in a shimmering burgundy dress, joining fellow attendees such as Alex Consani, Kylie Jenner, Nicole Kidman, and Paris Hilton.

Courtesy of Gucci, the event’s sponsor, Kardashian’s floor-sweeping sequin look was at once modest and revealing—with long sleeves and a turtleneck bodice contrasted by side cutouts and an open back. The All’s Fair star gave the look a moody, smokey-eye glam, long tousled hair, and a color-matched manicure.

Welcoming everyone from models to actors to philanthropists to musicians to athletes, the gala celebrated its 15th year this evening, supporting its ongoing efforts to expand its film programming. And like every year, it was co-chaired by Leonardo DiCaprio and LACMA trustee Eva Chow. It honored the work of painter Vija Celmins, known for her photo-realistic work that explores the complexity of nature, as well as Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve. Blackpink’s Rosé was tapped for a musical performance.

Kardashian first attended the Art+Film Gala over a decade ago, showing up to the 2014 edition with Kanye West. And the next year, just one month before the couple welcomed son Saint West, she made her sophomore appearance in a sheer black dress that highlighted her baby bump. The Skims founder continued to support the museum, finding time for the fundraiser in 2017, 2018, 2022, 2023, and 2024.

#6786. Kylie Jenner’s Deer-Print Ashi Studio Gown Is an Unexpected (and Welcome) Surprise

From leopard-print coats to zebra bikinis, Kylie Jenner has never shied away from an animal print. But at the Los Angeles County Museum (LACMA) Art+Film Gala, she made the case for a something a little unexpected.

Joined by the likes of Alex Consani, Paris Hilton, and Nicole Kidman, Jenner arrived at the museum and stopped for photos in front of Chris Burden’s famed public art installation, Urban Light, which doubled as a red carpet for the evening. There, among the oversize street lights, she was seen wearing a low-back Ashi Studio gown in a brown-and-silver deer print.

The piece, pulled from the house’s Fall/Winter 2026 couture collection and styled by Alexandra Rose and Mackenzie Grandquist, was stitched from precisely-cut panels of fabric to fit snug around the body. The skintight number featured a halter neckline and an open back, and from the knees, it relaxed into a long, floor-sweeping skirt. A dramatic tassel detail finished things off.

The evening marked Jenner’s first time attending the LACMA Art+Film Gala, which held its inaugural edition back in 2011. The event was founded to support the museum’s ongoing efforts to expand its programming, making film more central to its exhibitions and education. Like always, this year’s version welcomed everyone from models to actors to philanthropists to musicians to athletes, bringing together the biggest names in the worlds of art, film, fashion, and entertainment. Once again, Gucci signed on as the sponsor, and Leonardo DiCaprio and LACMA trustee Eva Chow served as co-chairs.

#6785. Few Bags Have Had the Staying Power of Balenciaga’s Le City—Now It’s Turning 25

It’s hard to believe that 25 years have passed since Balenciaga’s Le City bag arrived on the scene—the design riffing on a motorcycle jacket, the sans-logo attitude unapologetically cool. A quarter-century is long enough that some see the bag mostly with nostalgia while others are discovering its It-status for the first time.

Certainly, in the midst of the mythic maison’s creative director shakeup—the departure of Pierpaolo Piccioli, the appointment of Martine Rose—Le City remains an enduring constant, riding out every era from its creation by Nicolas Ghesquière through Alexander Wang and Demna, who proposed his own version, the Neo City, in 2020.

Starting tomorrow, Balenciaga is kicking off Le City’s anniversary with celebratory activations in several cities around the world. Le City House will bow in its Paris hometown for nine days, with New York, Tokyo, Shanghai, Beijing, and Seoul staggered through the end of the year. The spaces also exist to launch a major collaboration involving the artist provocateur Damien Hirst. Folks, get ready for DAMIENCIAGA, a limited edition Le City capsule that transposes some of his famous works to the characteristic Arena leather.

A few days prior to the reveal, I made a site visit to the historic address of 10, Avenue George V, where Cristobal established his atelier and where customers more recently could purchase Demna’s Couture. Le City House is altogether different: a multi-modal, Y2K-coded experience that is sleek yet visitor-friendly and daresay playful.

Upon entering, a prototype of Le City from 2001—compact and in brown cotton canvas—sits in a see-through cube atop a Parisian bench painted glossy blue. There’s a floor-to-ceiling display of Le City as eye candy: bags in vivid shades of Maldives Green and Ultra Violet; in surface treatments such as tweed panels and brogue trims; and in novelty one-offs (including Ghesquière’s Multicolor City Mondriaan in red, yellow, and blue). Nearby are the “closets” that boast bags belonging to celebrity collectors such as Nicole Ritchie, the French footballer Hugo Ekitike, Clémence Poésy and Isabelle Huppert (each Le City House will feature different boldface names) propped with daily items and old Blackberry devices that double as labels (Ritchie’s, for instance, is from 2005). Small screens flash Parisian landmarks while a full-length panel rotates editorial, street style, and paparazzi photos. For all the glimpses of Kate Moss, Chloe Sevigny, Mary-Kate Olsen, and Sienna Miller, Le City is clearly the star.

Further back, past a metal railing bedecked with padlocks is the room with Hirst’s creations. The most rarefied, done by hand, is doused in splashes of pigment like his Spin Paintings and exists as an edition of 25. The others—his multicolored spots arranged like a butterfly; his mandala of wings; his uniform grid of dots; and a compilation of his ideas as embroidered patches—will be more widely available.

The second space, dubbed “Le Salon,” functions like a leather workshop-turned-bag spa. Artisans stationed on Platner stools will be personalizing bags: replacing the lacing along the top handle, offering custom charms, and hand-painting or etching initials on the rectangular pocket mirror that has remained one of Le City’s defining details. People can also make an appointment to have their old bags assessed for extra refresh services.

Finally, there is a photo kiosk programmed as though straight out of a teen magazine quiz circa the 1990s, only that the theme is not crushes or careers, but which Le City is right for you. One result might yield Le City Moto (“Bold, confident and a little rebellious”); another Le City Mini Backpack (“Your match understands that you have your hands full”). Alas, you do not actually receive a free bag.

If Le City House represents a fun, public-facing commemoration of Balenciaga’s best-selling bag, the maison’s vast archive on the outskirts of Paris offers the contextual perspective. This is where, thanks to a tour provided by Heritage and Cultural Director, Gaspard de Massé, I found myself learning about how the Le City—eschewing conspicuous branding but rather adorned with a sexy mix of laces, buckles, and studs—almost never came to be.

Nicolas Ghesquière with the Balenciaga city bag in 2004. Photographed by Robert Fairer, Vogue, September 2004

As the lore goes and he recounts, Ghesquière was working on a motorcycle-inspired bag in 2000 when Moss saw a version and showed interest in it. He gave her one and offered others to his inner circle—women like Marie-Amélie Sauvé, Carine Roitfeld, and Emmanuelle Alt—initially calling it Le Lariat, then Le Motorcycle. Le First and Le City followed based on their sizes, until eventually, the latter stuck for the entire family.

The 3,000-square-meter temperature- and humidity-controlled space is filled not only with the kind of heaving mobile shelving units found in institutional archives, but also the storage of patrimonial furniture, Cristobal’s actual library, and two stunning paintings positioned upright (one is by Bernard Buffet of his wife, Annabel, wearing a pink Balenciaga gown; the other, surprisingly, is of Gabrielle Chanel in a soigné white ensemble by A.M. Cassandre).

Of course, we end up over at the units stacked with Le City models, never carried and originating from the workshops. You need not be prone to It-bag lust to marvel over the sheer number and variety—some 879 at last count. Dream of a shade and it’s probably in the mix. There are evolutions and iterations: the burnished studs that morphed to resemble thimbles; the brogue trims that evoked Derby shoes; the metal hardware; the Part Time with its seam down the middle or the square Velo format (presumably to fit inside a bicycle basket).

So how, in De Massé’s mind, has Le City remained such a hero piece? “I think it’s extremely identifiable, and because of that, it doesn’t really feel like taking a risk,” he says. “You know that you’re buying this particular bag for a specific reason; and undoubtedly, part of that reason is that you’re joining all those other people who already own one. There’s something of a community spirit around it; it’s not an exclusively ultra-luxury community, nor is it mass market. It occupies this interesting space somewhere in between.”

He goes on: “For today’s generations, it can also function as a kind of madeleine de Proust, something that evokes a particular moment or memory. I remember Britney Spears in the 2000s, for example. Even if I didn’t personally experience that period in the same way, those images are part of my imagination, and the bag allows me to reconnect with an aesthetic or a moment that I liked. There’s something reassuring about that. Of course, it’s different for everyone; but I think that recognizability, combined with the fact that the bag feels approachable and accessible, is fundamental to its success.”

Indeed, few bags have had such staying power independent of the promotion machine, off-duty model shot, or hype cycle. But Le City is a bag that also happens to wear well. The non-boxy shape proved easy to carry and the Arena leather already appeared lived-in, becoming more cherished as it was subjected to life’s vicissitudes. Remember Mary-Kate’s endless attachment to her mint green bag—not despite, but possibly because of, its glaring red wine stain?

Although Le City has never needed reinvention, it was updated in 2024 when various vintage styles were studied together, so that the new construction—hand-assembled from 25 panels—signified a faithful “amalgamation.” The launch was announced with a campaign of portraits by Mario Sorrenti starring Moss as well as Mona Tougaard, Juyeon, and Yang Chaoyue. Last year, an “ultra-luxe” version marked the first runway appearance of Le City, coinciding with Piccioli’s debut. Another campaign followed, this time by David Sims—Le City’s original fashion photographer—marking a reunion and full-circle moment.

The campaign for the Hirst series features Ritchie dressed in a draped yellow top over jeans, her gaze smoldering as the mandala butterfly bag hangs from her forearm. Ekitike cradles one of the patchwork styles alongside the Seine.

For Hirst, Le City was imprinted on his mind even before the collaboration opportunity arose. “I think everyone knows it, don’t they? It’s one of the most iconic bags of the last 25 years,” he tells Vogue via email. “You associate it with the noughties, with Kate Moss, yet it’s still remained so relevant.”

This is a whole other Hirst than when he was preserving sharks in tanks or encrusting skulls with diamonds, yet the bags are not without a hint of subversion seeing as the original Spot Paintings were named after pharmaceutical drugs or chemical compounds and the Butterfly mandalas alluded to mortality, spirituality, and the passage of time.

Hugo Ekitike with the Balenciaga “DAMIENCIAGA” bag.

It’s likely his 25 hand-painted Le Cities (or is it Les Citys?) will have collector value. They look like they were a thrill to make, the layers of vivid paint leaving barely a trace of original surface. The artist suggests the best part will be when people make the bags their own. “It’s not just a ‘Balenciaga’ or a ‘Hirst’… they’re adding their personality to it. And I think that’s what fashion is all about.”

They are also a reminder that fashion loves a revival. Each Le City House will be reintroducing people to a cultural moment well before quiet luxury, and whatever we are shifting into now. Thanks to the anniversary, the bag is definitely back; the bolder, the better. To wit, Le City x Hirst even boasts a logo of sorts: ‘Damienciaga’ appears in a fine silver script along one side.

#6781. 9 Best Eyeliners for Older Women That Glide on With Ease

When I shop for eyeliner these days, I feel like I’m going into a restaurant with a list of dietary restrictions. I have always had hooded eyes, but at 46, the hooding is more pronounced. I have sensitive eyes, too, and fine lines starting to set in. In short, I’m looking for an eyeliner to play up my gaze while downplaying any discomfort or signs of aging. It’s a balancing act, to be sure, but it’s one that the best eyeliners for older women can accomplish with finesse—and if it becomes tempting to skip eyeliner altogether, consider this advice from a pro: “Eyeliner actually becomes more important as we age,” says makeup artist Stevi Christine. “Lashes tend to thin over time, and a liner at the roots helps bring back that youthful fullness.”

Since I’ve found a few formulas that I swear by—including the Laura Mercier pencil that’s on this list—I see what Christine means. On days when I do wear eyeliner, I look more awake, chipper, and polished than on days when I don’t. The trick? Finding formulas that are not only flattering, but gentle on the eyes. Formulas for older women should also be easy to apply and remove without tugging at the lids. Ahead, find the eyeliners that check every box.

What type of eyeliner is best for mature eyes?

“Because of its rich color payoff, a smooth gel or cream eyeliner pencil is a great choice for enhancing mature eyes,” says Wagener. “Eyeliner with a creamy texture glides on effortlessly, providing a defined line that won’t tug at delicate skin.” On the other hand, Wagener tells her mature clients to steer clear of most liquid felt-tip liners. “They can be less forgiving and very difficult to use,” she says.

What to Look for in an Eyeliner for Older Women

When it comes to choosing an eyeliner for women over 50, makeup artists keep a few key factors in mind.

How should you apply eyeliner to mature eyes?

“Depending on the eye shape, I often line only the outer third or outer half of the upper lash line and then tightline the whole length of the lash line from underneath,” says Patinkin. “This is a great technique for lots of reasons.” First, she says, it contributes to a lifted look at the outer corner of the eyes, where the shadow is thicker. The technique also helps define the shape of the eyes without “eating up lid space,” she says. Tightlining is another technique makeup artists favor for mature eyes. “It makes the lashes look thicker because you’re filling in gaps between the roots of the lashes,” Patinkin says.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity makeup artists—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to eyeliners for older women, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, eyeliner type, shade range, and ease of application. To do this, we paired our tester feedback on each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you.

#6778. Princess Kate Pairs Her Polka-Dot Midi Dress With a Meaningful Pair of Family Jewels

She and Prince William attended the Festival of Remembrance event in London

Every year, the Festival of Remembrance welcomes people from all over the country to Royal Albert Hall for an evening of celebration, honoring active members of the military, veterans, and all the families who have lost loved ones in the armed forces. With musical performances and personal testimonies, the Saturday evening event kicks off Remembrance Sunday, the official day of remembrance in the United Kingdom.

As always, members of the royal family made an appearance at the annual festival. But this year saw a particularly strong turnout, with King Charles III and Queen Camilla in attendance, as well as Prince William and Princess Kate.

For the occasion, Kate, always intentional with her style choices, put together a look full of meaningful pieces fitting for such a meaningful event. Her black-and-white polka-dot dress, for starters, was the same piece worn to Prince Philip’s memorial service back in 2022. Courtesy of Alessandra Rich, it featured a high mock neckline and long sleeves, with a drop-waist pleated midi skirt and a black belt accent. The princess updated the piece by adding a red poppy—the symbol of remembrance—and her silver Irish Guards regimental brooch, which represented her role as Colonel of the Irish Guards.

For jewelry, the future queen brought a piece of her late grandmother-in-law with her, wearing a sparkling pair of diamond earrings that once belonged to Queen Elizabeth II. The statement jewels featured a cluster of diamonds that created a floral-shaped stud, from which an additional strand of diamonds hung, framed by an outer oval frame of... yes, more diamonds.

#6777. Around the World in 80 Handbags—Inside a New Istanbul Exhibition Devoted to the Exceptional Accessory

A handbag is rarely just a handbag. It can be a keeper of secrets, a declaration of status, or a traveling companion—not to mention a rather expensive place to keep one’s keys. At Beymen Tersane, Istanbul’s newest shopping destination, it takes on another role: that of a vessel for cultural memory. This idea lies at the heart of “Timeless Treasures—The Eternal Journey of the Bag,” an exhibition inaugurated to mark the cultural complex’s opening, bringing together 80 creations from 55 international brands in a dialogue between contemporary design and the layered heritage of Anatolia and the Ottoman Empire.

Curated by Laurence Benaïm, the presentation is less an exercise in historical illustration than an invitation to look at memory through a different perspective. The challenge, she explained, was not to reproduce traditional motifs or reduce Ottoman references to decorative shorthand, but to translate their spirit into a modern design language. Her vision was that of a “curiosity cabinet of dreams and craftsmanship,” where newly commissioned pieces sit alongside archival treasures from the likes of Dior, Louis Vuitton, and Schiaparelli.

The journey unfolds across seven chapters, each exploring a different facet of the relationship between bags and cultural memory. Precious Envelopes includes the pouches once used by ambassadors to carry letters, imperial decrees and secrets, a reminder that the art of keeping things under wraps has a long history. Heavenly Gardens draws on the flora and fauna of İznik ceramics and Ottoman palace gardens, while Golden Jewels explores the allure of gold. Magical Boxes considers the bag as guardian of private possessions and hidden treasures, a function that has hardly lost its appeal. Nomad Memories traces the weaving, leatherwork, and saddlebag traditions that traveled from Central Asia to Anatolia. A final glance towards the future brings in three designs by young Turkish talents, selected through a competition supported by Beymen in collaboration with local universities. Among the historical highlights is a piece of luxurious archaeology: a massive Louis Vuitton wardrobe trunk, made in 1886 at the Maison’s Asnières atelier for Sultan Abdülhamid II.

A massive Louis Vuitton wardrobe trunk, made in 1886 at the Maison’s Asnières atelier for Sultan Abdülhamid II.

For Benaïm, the point is that heritage should not be treated as a fixed inheritance or an exercise in nostalgia. “Heritage isn’t about looking backwards. It’s about carrying the beauty of the past into the future,” she remarked. The exhibition, more than two years in the making, is a “love letter to Turkish culture” and an exploration of the ways in which fashion can preserve cultural memory while giving it new meaning. “There is no luxury without soul, without heart and without love, and without a sense of time,” Benaïm added.

The choice of venue is not incidental. Beymen Tersane occupies part of the historic shipyard on the Golden Horn, a site stretching back some 600 years, reimagined by Rem Koolhaas’s OMA as a 12,000-square-meter destination for fashion, art, and lifestyle. Rather than imposing another conventional department-store interior on the monumental structure, the architects conceived a horizontal sequence of eight galleries.

“Timeless Treasures—The Eternal Journey of the Bag,” features bags by 55 international brands including newly commissioned pieces and archival treasures from the likes of Dior, Louis Vuitton, and Schiaparelli.

For Beymen Group CEO Elif Çapçı, the project continues the conversation started in 2023 with “Golden Opulence,” a 50th anniversary exhibition in which 50 international brands were commissioned for a unique piece. This time, the bag became the focus, “an object whose changing form and function offers a revealing record of shifting lifestyles, tastes and social codes,” Çapçı noted.

Rachid Mohamed Rachid, CEO of Mayhoola and chairman of Beymen, sees Beymen Tersane as part of a broader ambition to bring the cultural complexities of Turkey to the attention of the international luxury world. But there is something deeper at stake here than a showcase of commercial partnerships. “As Istanbul has always understood, the most interesting exchanges happen when different worlds meet without either having to surrender its identity,” he said.

And perhaps this is the point: The handbag, after all, is a meeting place of its own, a repository of craftsmanship, memory, and imagination. There is clearly more to it than what fits inside. Though isn’t it nice that it also accommodates a phone, a lipstick and a pair of sunglasses?

“Timeless Treasures—The Eternal Journey of the Bag” is on view at Istanbul’s Beymen Tersane through February 8, 2027.

Istanbul’s Beyman Tersane shopping destination.

#6773. The Vogue Business People Moves Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business People Moves Tracker, a running list highlighting the key executive appointments and exits across the fashion and beauty industries. From CEOs to creative directors to other key C-suite hires, we track the leadership shifts that are reshaping the industry.

Background: Caroline Deroche Pasquier joins Dior in a newly created role as director of press, VIP and cultural relations. She began her career at Saint Laurent before joining LVMH, where she worked at Louis Vuitton and Givenchy. During the last six years, Pasquier has led global communications for Bottega Veneta and then Versace. At Dior, she will work closely with the house’s creative director Jonathan Anderson, reporting to Olivier Bialobos, deputy managing director in charge of global communication and image.

Company comments: “[Deroche Pasquier’s] career spans communication, creative collaboration, international markets and cultural relationships, giving her a broad perspective on the development and expression of luxury brands,” the company said in a statement.

Background: Oliver Timm has voluntarily stepped down from Hugo Boss, where he’s been both chief sales officer and deputy CEO since 2024, as well as the company board. In the meantime, CEO Daniel Grieder, alongside CFO and COO Ivica Maric, will split Timm’s previous duties. Timm was initially appointed as chief sales officer in 2021, to oversee Hugo Boss’s two brands (Boss and Hugo), including wholesale, e-commerce, visual merchandizing, retail operations, and customer relations.

The announcement follows Hugo Boss’s 5% sales drop in Q3 — attributed to an ongoing turnaround at the company — and Frasers Group’s de-facto takeover of the company on October 23.

Company comments: “Oliver Timm and I have been working side by side throughout our careers for almost 30 years, and it is a great honor for me to look back on this time and the many moments we have shared. I will miss working alongside him,” said Grieder in a statement. “During his time at Hugo Boss, he has repositioned sales with a future-oriented omnichannel approach and a strong customer-centric mindset, making a significant contribution to our growth and digitalization. As I look back at these achievements, I wish him, also on behalf of the entire managing board, the very best for the future.”

Michael Murray, Hugo Boss chair and Frasers Group CEO, also shared his appreciation: “On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to thank Oliver Timm for his contribution to Hugo Boss over the past years. We appreciate his commitment and wish him all the best for his professional and personal future.”

Background: Ben Hallam, most recently SVP of marketing at Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts, has been appointed as Lululemon’s chief brand officer. At the sportswear brand, Hallam will lead global brand marketing, brand creative, store experience, and community. He will join the company’s senior leadership team and report to CEO Heidi O’Neill who joined in April 2026.

The announcement comes after the appointments of Maggie Gauger as president and chief product officer and Joseph Godsey as chief operating officer. On Friday, the company also announced the appointment of Emily Sunderland as chief strategy officer, effective November 23. Sunderland joins from Boston Consulting Group and will report to chief financial officer Meghan Frank. Searches remain underway for a chief technology officer and a chief communications officer.

Company comments: “Ben brings an exceptional combination of creative vision, commercial discipline, and experience transforming iconic, premium brands at scale,” O’Neill said in a statement. “His proven ability to translate brand strategy into distinctive and compelling guest experiences will be critical as we strengthen how our brand comes to life across every touchpoint. Ben will play a central role in building a stronger and more competitive Lululemon.”

Background: Daisy Shaw-Ellis has been appointed CMO of Malone Souliers, where she will oversee the brand’s global marketing and communications, with an emphasis on expansion in North America. Shaw-Ellis joins from Condé Nast, where she was most recently accessories and jewelry director for Vogue and Vanity Fair.

Company comments: “We are delighted to welcome Daisy to Malone Souliers as global chief marketing officer,” CEO Andrew Wright said in a statement. “Her experience in executive positions at some of the industry’s most established and influential titles, alongside her exceptional eye and proven track record in luxury brand-building, will both enhance and amplify our voice globally. This is a pivotal moment for Malone Souliers as we embark on a new and exciting trajectory, and we look forward to presenting the brand in new and exciting ways in the coming seasons.”

Background: Clarisse Godbillon, who was CFO and COO of Lemaire from 2020 to 2025, is returning to the brand as managing director. She left Lemaire in 2025 to become COO of Jacquemus, and made the move back to the French label after Laetitia Mergui stepped down from the head job earlier this year.

Company comments: “Clarisse possesses an in-depth understanding of the company’s various activities and a profound knowledge of its identity,” the house said in a statement. “As managing director, she will oversee the development of the brand and lead its strategic and operational direction, working closely with [the house’s artistic directors and majority shareholders] Christophe Lemaire and Sarah-linh Tran.”

Background: Lady Gaga has moved into the CEO role at Haus Labs, the clean beauty company she founded in 2019. This comes after co-founder and former CEO Ben Jones exited the brand in early October. Gaga will now lead all commercial aspects of Haus Labs, alongside her prior responsibilities of creative direction and product development.

Background: Ryan Lally has been promoted to chief brand communications officer at Ralph Lauren Corp. Formerly SVP of global public relations and brand communications, Lally will continue to build on the company’s global comms strategy in this newly created role, while overseeing talent partnerships, events and more. Lally has been with the company for more than two decades, and will continue to report to David Lauren, chief branding and innovation officer.

Background: Alexis Hoopes, formerly global fashion VP at Ebay, has joined The RealReal as chief merchandising officer. At Ebay, she led the company’s $10 billion global fashion business for two-plus years, including the expansion of its Authenticity Guarantee program to new categories, price points and markets, strengthening trust among buyers and sellers. Hoopes will now lead The RealReal’s merchandising strategy, focusing on its luxury assortment and personalized product discovery — as the platform further advances its AI capabilities and unlocks growth opportunities.

Company comments: “Alexis is a proven leader who brings a rare combination of luxury merchandising expertise, global marketplace experience and operational discipline,” Rati Sahi Levesque, president and CEO of The RealReal, said in a statement. “As we build on our leadership in luxury resale, her ability to connect exceptional merchandise with evolving consumer demand will be instrumental in accelerating growth.”

Background: Hector Muelas joined LVMH in 2015 as global VP of content and creative, after working for Apple. Between 2017 and 2019, he was chief brand officer of LVMH-owned luggage brand Rimowa under chief executive Alexandre Arnault. Muelas then returned to Apple as global group creative director in 2019, a role he held until 2021. He returned to LVMH in 2023 as Tiffany & Co.’s global chief brand and creative officer, reuniting with Alexandre Arnault.

He has now been named Louis Vuitton chief brand creative officer, a newly created position reporting to Louis Vuitton deputy CEO Damien Bertrand.

Company comments: “Hector will define and steer our creative storytelling across all touchpoints, thereby ensuring strong overall image consistency. Leading creative and content execution, he will oversee all brand campaigns, with the art buying team led by Magena Chansarel and the content factory team led by Carole Fuchs joining his organization. In close collaboration with our business units, regions, and creative talents, Hector will further elevate our brand desirability, ensuring the house continues to set the benchmark in cultural resonance, creative boldness, and emotional connection with our clients worldwide,” Bertrand said in an internal announcement.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky, who most recently exited the board at Chanel, but remains president of Chanel SAS and fashion, is now co-chair of The Fashion Pact. A non-profit organization, The Fashion Pact is a coalition of CEOs from more than 150 companies representing a third of the global fashion industry by volume. Pavlovsky will work alongside Inditex CEO Óscar García Maceiras and climate campaigner Paul Polman to build on the work of the pact in creating a net-zero fashion industry. (Chanel is among the coalition’s founding signatories back in 2019.)

Company comments: “As we look ahead to 2027, our focus is increasingly on translating collective ambition into implementation, and scaling solutions across the industry. Bruno’s appointment marks an important step in this journey, bringing valuable leadership and perspective as we work to strengthen collaboration across regions, business models and supply chains,” The Fashion Pact wrote on LinkedIn.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky joined Chanel in 1990 and became a board member in 2018, a duty he will now step down from. Since 2022, he has also been president of the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode. Pavlovsky remains president of Chanel SAS and of the house’s fashion activities.

Company comments: “This latest move marks the completion of the board’s evolution toward a composition of independent directors, bringing diverse external expertise and perspectives, while retaining executive representation through the global executive chair and global CEO. Bruno Pavlovsky remains fully committed to his role as president of Chanel’s fashion activities and president of Chanel SAS,” Chanel said in a statement.

Background: Zankov has appointed Jack Tobin, founder of luxury brand development consultancy Jack Tobin Agency, as CEO and business partner of Zankov, formalizing a partnership that has developed since Tobin began consulting for the brand two years ago. Since beginning its partnership with Jack Tobin Agency, Zankov has increased its international business more than tenfold and doubled its global stockist network.

Company comments: “Zankov is at an incredibly exciting stage in its growth. I have always envisioned having a partner who could join me in shaping the next chapter of the brand — someone who shares my ambition to build an enduring business while staying true to the creative vision that has always defined Zankov. Jack is the ideal partner to take this next step with, and I’m excited about what we can build together,” says Henry Zankov, founder and creative director.

Background: Net-a-Porter (NAP) has appointed Devina Foley as Americas president to oversee the retailer’s US and Canada strategy. With more than 20 years of experience across retail, merchandising and e-commerce, Foley will help strengthen NAP’s market positioning as it settles into a new era under LuxExperience Group. She has held senior leadership roles at Bandier, Rockets of Awesome and Gilt, following earlier positions at Loft and Gap Inc. Based in New York, Foley will report to NAP CEO Heather Kaminetsky.

Company comments: “Devina brings an impressive breadth of experience and a proven track record of driving growth and leading businesses through transformation,” Kaminetsky said in a statement. “Her leadership and expertise will be invaluable as we continue to grow Net-a-Porter’s US business.”

Background: LVMH has promoted Clara Boissonnas, formerly women’s leather goods product director at Louis Vuitton, to CEO of Pucci. Boissonnas joined Louis Vuitton in 2002 as a product manager, before exiting four years later. After a decade working across Lanvin and Byredo, she returned to LV where she helped shape the maison’s coveted leather goods business.
